What changes, and when

The arrangement is a mutual exemption from the visa requirement, agreed between foreign ministers Gideon Sa’ar and Omar Bula Escobar and announced by Israel’s foreign ministry. It takes effect on 1 September 2026. Colombia’s Cancillería had published no statement or decree of its own by the end of 20 August.

The stated purpose is ordinary enough: tourism, business travel and commercial exchange. Colombia has been trying to widen its tourism base beyond North America and Europe for years, and Israel sends a large number of long-stay travellers to South America, particularly young people travelling after military service. Until July 2025, when the two countries dropped their reciprocal exemption, Colombia was one of the easier stops on that circuit.

One practical caution. The announcement was made on 20 August. If you are travelling before 1 September, the old requirements still apply. Check with the consulate rather than assuming.

How Colombia got here in two years

In May 2024, President Gustavo Petro severed diplomatic relations with Israel over the war in Gaza, which he described as a genocide. Colombia had been one of Israel’s closest defence partners in Latin America, and the break was not symbolic — it touched arms procurement, intelligence sharing and coal exports.

Petro’s term ended on 7 August 2026. His successor, Abelardo de la Espriella, campaigned on restoring the relationship and re-established ties immediately; on 14 August he separately dismissed five ambassadors appointed by Petro who had declined to submit protocol resignations. A decree to end the ban on coal exports to Israel is ready.

The visa waiver is the piece of that reversal most likely to affect ordinary people rather than governments.

What it means if you live in Colombia

If you hold Colombian citizenship, you get back a destination you could reach paperwork-free until July 2025. If you hold Israeli citizenship and are among the foreign residents in Medellín, Bogotá or Santa Marta, your family can visit without a consular appointment again.

For businesses, the effect is smaller but real. Israel is a significant buyer of Colombian coal and coffee and a significant seller of agricultural technology, water systems and security equipment. Removing the visa step does not create trade on its own, but it removes friction from the visits that precede trade.

There is also a tourism angle worth watching. Colombia’s Caribbean coast and coffee region already draw a steady Israeli backpacker flow that currently routes through Peru and Bolivia. Making entry simpler will move some of that volume.

The Colombia Israel visa waiver still has open questions

Several details have not been published. No Colombian decree number has appeared, and neither government has said how long visa-free stays will last. The arrangement that ran until July 2025 gives the benchmark: Colombians entered Israel for up to 90 days, and Israelis could spend up to 180 cumulative days in Colombia in any 365.

Nor is it clear whether the waiver covers all passport types or only ordinary passports. Diplomatic and service passports are usually handled separately.

And the wider relationship is still moving. Colombia has announced it will relocate its embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem — a step far more contentious at home and abroad than a visa arrangement — and has recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. Sa’ar has described the direction of travel as a return to a strategic alliance.

For now, though, the practical takeaway is simple. From 1 September, one fewer form.

How this fits Colombia’s wider reopening

The visa move is not happening in isolation. Since taking office, the De la Espriella government has replaced ambassadors, floated a tax reform it has yet to publish, and had to declare an economic emergency after the 10 August earthquake, whose preliminary damage bill Colombia puts at US$9.57 billion.

In that context, a visa waiver is cheap diplomacy. It costs the treasury nothing, it delivers a visible result within weeks, and it signals to Washington and Jerusalem that Colombia’s foreign policy has changed direction without requiring a single peso of new spending.

Whether it lasts is a different question. Colombia’s relationship with Israel swung hard in one direction under Petro and has swung hard back within a month of the new government taking office. Anyone planning travel or business on the strength of it should keep that volatility in mind: this exemption has now been scrapped once and reinstated once inside fourteen months, and nothing about the arrangement makes it harder to reverse a third time.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the Colombia Israel visa waiver start? On 1 September 2026. The agreement was announced on 20 August 2026 and does not apply to travel before that date. Does the waiver apply to both countries’ citizens? Yes. It is a mutual exemption, covering Israelis travelling to Colombia and Colombians travelling to Israel. Why did Colombians need a visa for Israel in the first place? They did not, until July 2025. Gustavo Petro severed diplomatic ties in May 2024 over the war in Gaza and the mutual visa exemption was dropped the following year. Abelardo de la Espriella restored relations after taking office on 7 August 2026.

Sources: La República — Colombia and Israel drop visa requirement; Semana — visa requirement eliminated; Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs

World.title: Costa Rica Expands Online English Classes to 100 Rural Schools
World.content:
More than 2,000 children in rural Costa Rican communities are now receiving English lessons through a technology-based program that connects small schools with specialized teachers. The program, called Hummingbird, has grown from an initial test in 35 schools to 100 schools across the country, according to the Ministry of Public Education (MEP).

Hummingbird is aimed at rural schools that may not have their own English teacher. Students receive live online lessons from a trained English instructor, while their regular teacher remains in the classroom to provide in-person help. The classes use computers, tablets and interactive whiteboards. Along with learning English, students gain experience using digital tools that are becoming increasingly important in school and the workplace.

The program is led by MEP and the Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (MICITT), with support from the National University (UNA) and the Rural Development Institute (INDER). Officials say the goal is to give rural children access to the same learning opportunities available at larger schools, where specialized teachers are generally easier to find.

MICITT Minister Paula Bogantes Zamora and MEP Academic Vice Minister María Alexandra Ulate recently visited León Cortés Castro School in San Marcos de Tarrazú to see how the classes work and speak with students and teachers. Bogantes said technology should be used to close educational gaps and prevent a child’s home community from limiting what they can learn.

Ulate said cooperation among government agencies, schools and local communities can help overcome the distance separating rural students from specialized instruction. The program has also received support from parents. Juan Carlos Mora, president of the Cuesta de Moras School Board of Education, said Hummingbird has shown that children can receive English instruction even when their school is far from the larger population centers.

For students, the program offers practical preparation for high school, where English becomes a more important part of the curriculum. “My favorite word is sharpener, which means maquinilla; it was the first word I learned with teacher Marcos,” Cuesta de Moras student Nichson Navarro said.

The government has not released detailed information about the program’s cost, the complete list of participating schools or how students’ English progress will be measured. However, officials say Hummingbird is part of a broader effort to use internet connections and digital equipment to improve education in communities where access to specialized teachers remains limited.

World.title: Costa Rica Documentary Reveals Why Whales From Two Hemispheres Choose Golfo Dulce
World.content:
There is one stretch of water on the planet where humpback whales from the far north and the far south both come to give birth, and it sits at the southern tip of Costa Rica. Golfo Dulce, the deep inlet that separates the Osa Peninsula from the mainland, receives mothers that have swum up from the freezing waters off Antarctica and mothers that have come down the Pacific coast of North America. Nowhere else do the two populations overlap. Researchers who worked on a new Costa Rican documentary about the gulf call it the womb of the Pacific.

That documentary, Costa Rica, Cradle of Whales, premiered Wednesday night on Canal 7 as the first episode of a revived nature strand called El Planeta Azul, or The Blue Planet. The full film went online free after broadcast. The production took three years. Camera teams worked in Golfo Dulce and in Bahía Ballena, the bay farther north where the whale watching industry is concentrated, filming in high definition and 4K with drones, underwater cameras and hydrophones to record the animals’ songs. Broadcaster Teletica describes it as the first wildlife documentary produced entirely in house.

Director María Jesús Prada leads the project alongside marine biologist Frank Garita, producer Eddy Vargas and editor Rigoberto Quirós. Biologists were embedded in the production team rather than consulted afterward, and the broadcaster says every factual claim in the film was checked against academic standards before it reached the screen.

“In Costa Rica we are privileged,” Garita said. He described two separate humpback populations that visit the country’s waters across nearly the entire year. The episode follows a mother and her calf through the stages that make the journey so costly. Humpbacks carry one of the longest gestations in the ocean, and a mother arriving in Costa Rican waters has typically not eaten for months. She nurses anyway, at a volume the film quantifies, while teaching her calf to breathe, dive and travel before the two of them turn around and swim back.

The film also takes on questions science has not settled. Humpbacks sing without vocal cords, and the documentary explains the mechanism. Male song changes from season to season across an entire population, and here the film is careful to separate what researchers have measured from what they still cannot explain.

Accounts of the migration itself vary. Material released on premiere day put the journey at more than 8,000 kilometers (about 4,970 miles), while an earlier description gave roughly 9,000 kilometers (about 5,590 miles), and organizers of the annual whale festival in Osa have used a figure of up to 8,400 kilometers (about 5,220 miles). The northern population’s starting point is also described inconsistently, as Alaska in one account and as the coasts of Oregon and California in others.

The timing of the premiere is not accidental. Costa Rica is in the middle of the southern hemisphere season now, which runs roughly from mid-July into November and peaks in August and September. A second season built around northern hemisphere whales opens in December and runs into April, giving the country one of the longest whale watching windows anywhere.

If you want to see them yourself, book a morning departure. Seas are calmest early and the animals are more active, and most tours out of Bahía Uvita run three to four hours, often with a stop at the sandbar that emerges at low tide in the shape of a whale’s tail.

Choose an operator with an environmental permit. The permit exists because boats that crowd or chase a nursing pair can push a calf away from its mother, and a calf that loses contact in open water is in serious trouble. National rules also bar swimmers from entering the water while a cetacean is nearby, for the same reason.

The Whale and Dolphin Festival in Osa, which builds a weekend of boat tours, talks and community events around the peak of the season, is scheduled for early September, with organizers listing the fourth through the sixth. Discounted tours for residents are typically part of the program.

Golfo Dulce itself carries protections that predate the film. It is one of a small number of tropical fjords in the world, and in 2018 the government declared roughly 4,000 hectares (about 9,880 acres) of the northern gulf a no take sanctuary for scalloped hammerhead sharks, the first shark sanctuary in the country. The gulf was named a Mission Blue Hope Spot the following year, and Piedras Blancas National Park protects some 14,000 hectares (about 35,000 acres) of rainforest along its northeastern shore.

The episode is dedicated to Marco Picado Cozza, who pioneered nature programming at the broadcaster and died in 1996. Prada is his niece. El Planeta Azul is scheduled to return every three months with new films on Costa Rican wildlife and ecosystems.

For a place like ours that markets its biodiversity abroad more successfully than almost anywhere, homegrown wildlife filmmaking on this scale has been surprisingly rare. Whether the quarterly schedule holds will say something about how much appetite there is for it.

World.title: Man Allegedly Collected North American Woman’s Pension for 20 Years
World.content:
Costa Rican prosecutors are investigating a man suspected of collecting about $800,000 from the pension of a North American woman who died more than 20 years ago. The man, identified only by the last name Abarca, managed a home for older adults in La Uruca, San José. A North American woman with the last name Collins moved into the home in 1999 and lived there until her death in 2005. She was 78.

Authorities believe Abarca arranged for Collins to be buried in a cemetery in Cartago. The following year, he allegedly submitted false documents to the California State Teachers’ Retirement System, which manages pensions for public school educators in California. The documents allegedly made it appear that Abarca was legally authorized to manage Collins’ affairs, even though she was already dead. Investigators believe this allowed him to obtain a bank card and continue accessing her pension payments.

Prosecutors estimate that at least $800,000 was withdrawn between 2006 and 2026. The alleged scheme was discovered when the California retirement system tried to confirm whether Collins was still alive. The organization contacted the United States Embassy in Costa Rica, which confirmed that she had died in 2005.

Costa Rican authorities later searched Abarca’s home for evidence. The investigation involves suspected fraud, the use of false documents and placing false information in official paperwork. A court has ordered Abarca to report regularly to judicial authorities, keep a permanent address and remain in Costa Rica while the investigation continues. Those restrictions have reportedly been in place since July 25.

Prosecutors have not said whether any of the money has been recovered or whether the California pension system has requested repayment. The accusations have not been proven in court, and Abarca must be considered innocent unless he is convicted.

World.title: Costa Rica President Sends Eight Major Proposals to Congress
World.content:
President Laura Fernández has presented eight new bills that could change how Costa Rica handles pensions, loans, government contracts, internet funding and several other public programs. The proposals were announced as Fernández marked her first 100 days in office. However, none of the changes has taken effect. Each bill must first be discussed and approved by the Legislative Assembly.

Here is what the eight bills would do in simple terms:

Provide more pensions for people in need

The first bill would move part of an employer-paid payroll contribution into the fund that provides basic pensions to older adults and people with disabilities who did not pay enough into the regular pension system. The government estimates that the change could provide pensions to around 31,000 additional people.

The proposal would not take money from workers’ individual retirement accounts. Instead, it would redirect money currently sent to Banco Popular.

Limit some powers of the Comptroller General

Another bill would reduce the Comptroller General’s ability to stop or interfere with certain government projects and contracts. The Comptroller is responsible for checking how public money is spent. Under the proposal, its work would focus more narrowly on whether public funds are being handled legally.

Supporters may argue that this would help government projects move faster. Critics are likely to say it could weaken an important check on public spending. Similar ideas appeared in earlier “Jaguar” proposals, parts of which faced constitutional objections. This bill is therefore expected to receive close legal and political attention.

Allow faster government purchasing in special cases

The government also wants public institutions to have a quicker way to purchase goods or services when there is an urgent risk or when the usual bidding process does not fit the situation. An institution would have to explain why the normal process is unsuitable, how it selected the supplier, how much it will spend and how long the contract will last.

The Comptroller would then have 15 working days to review the request. A lack of response would not automatically mean approval.

Give INA more control over hiring

One proposal would create a separate employment system for the National Learning Institute, known as INA. Existing employees could remain under the current Civil Service system. New employees would enter the new system, while current workers could choose to transfer without losing the rights they have already earned.

INA’s board would also receive more freedom to create, remove and classify jobs. The government says this would help the institution respond more quickly to Costa Rica’s training and employment needs.

Move forward with Ciudad Gobierno

Another bill would create special rules for Ciudad Gobierno, a planned group of office buildings intended to bring dozens of government departments together in one location. The Finance Ministry could lease the buildings for up to 30 years, with the possibility of extending the agreement to a maximum of 50 years. The Central American Bank for Economic Integration, known as BCIE, would play a central role in developing the project.

The government says Ciudad Gobierno could save approximately $26 million a year by reducing the amount it pays to rent offices around San José. The proposal includes the possible relocation of as many as 35 public institutions and departments. Parts of the plan involving public land and property used by the Liceo de Costa Rica could become controversial.

Help farmers and fishers buy insurance

The sixth bill would create an agricultural insurance fund called Fonagro. The fund would help farmers, livestock producers, fishers and aquaculture businesses pay for insurance against losses caused by weather, disease and other emergencies.

Small producers and artisanal fishers could receive assistance covering up to 75% of their insurance premiums. Medium-sized producers could receive help covering up to 50%. Money for the program could come from the National Insurance Institute, the Agriculture Ministry and the Rural Development Institute, depending on available funds.

Change who manages money for internet access

The government wants to move responsibility for the National Telecommunications Fund, known as Fonatel, from the telecommunications regulator Sutel to Costa Rica’s Innovation and Research Promoter. Fonatel uses money collected from telecommunications companies to improve internet and telephone access in communities where private companies may not provide adequate service.

The Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications Ministry would also receive greater control over the annual fee paid by telecommunications companies. Existing Fonatel contracts and projects would remain valid during an 18-month transition.

Change how maximum interest rates are calculated

The final bill would change the system Costa Rica uses to set maximum legal interest rates. Costa Rica currently has a formula intended to prevent lenders from charging extremely high interest. Under the proposal, the financial regulator Sugef would calculate new limits each year using a method approved by Conassif, the country’s financial oversight council.

Different types of loans could have different limits. For example, credit cards, personal loans and small-business loans might no longer share the same maximum rate. The proposal would not immediately remove interest-rate limits. However, the new calculation method could result in some limits rising or falling. The final effect on borrowers would depend on the formula adopted by regulators.

What happens next?

The eight bills will now have to move through the Legislative Assembly. Lawmakers can approve, reject or change them during the process. Some proposals, particularly the plan to limit the Comptroller’s powers, may also face questions about whether they comply with Costa Rica’s Constitution.

For now, pensions, interest-rate limits, government purchasing rules and other programs remain unchanged.

World.title: Man accused of taking $7,500 for deliveries he allegedly never made walks free after charges withdrawn
World.content:
Man accused of taking $7,500 for deliveries he allegedly never made walks free after charges withdrawn

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-year-old supervisor accused of taking a $7,500 deposit for 40 loads of concrete mix that were allegedly never delivered walked free from court on Thursday after the complainant indicated that she no longer wished to pursue the case.

Romelo Lee Hernandez, of the Ladyville area, appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in Court #5, where he was charged with obtaining a money transfer by deception. Prosecutors alleged that on March 13, 2025, Hernandez received a $7,500 bank transfer from Maheia’s United Concrete & Supplies Ltd. as a 50 percent deposit toward the delivery of 40 loads of concrete mix, but the materials were never delivered and the money was not returned.

Hernandez pleaded not guilty to the charge.

However, the company’s administrative director appeared before the court and indicated that she did not wish to proceed with further court action against him.

In light of her request, the prosecution offered no further evidence and the charge against Hernandez was withdrawn. He was then free to leave the court.

According to the original complaint, the administrative director transferred $7,500 from the company’s Belize Bank account to an Atlantic Bank account in Hernandez’s name. The payment was reportedly intended as a deposit for concrete mix to be delivered to the company’s production plant at Mile 12¼ on the George Price Highway.

The administrative director later reported to police that the materials were not delivered as agreed. She alleged that Hernandez subsequently told her four loads were on the way, but they never arrived, and that he would instead return the money.

Police alleged that neither the materials nor the refund had been received when the complaint was made.

Hernandez was detained on Wednesday, August 19, 2026, and subsequently charged. With the complainant declining further court action, the case against him came to an end at Thursday’s arraignment.

World.title: Trinibad man remains on remand until he pays full outstanding $11,470 bill to Golden Bay Hotel
World.content:
Trinibad man remains on remand until he pays full outstanding $11,470 bill to Golden Bay Hotel

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Trinidadian national Rubindra Dale Rampersad will remain at the Belize Central Prison until at least August 28 after reaching a mediation agreement with Golden Bay Hotel to settle an outstanding bill of more than $11,000.

Rampersad, 46, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday represented by attorney Kimberly Wallace of Bradley’s Chambers, in the absence of attorney Darrell Bradley.

The court was informed that mediation between Rampersad and Golden Bay Hotel had resulted in an agreement under which he and his family will pay the hotel the full outstanding amount, approximately $11,470.24, on or before August 28, 2026. A representative of Golden Bay Hotel was present and confirmed the hotel’s agreement with the arrangement.

The Chief Magistrate accepted the mediation agreement and ordered that payment be made by the stipulated date. The prosecution has indicated that, once the terms of the agreement are satisfied, it intends to withdraw the criminal charge against Rampersad.

The matter was consequently adjourned until August 28. If the agreement is fulfilled, Rampersad is expected to be released and his passport, which has been held by the court as part of his bail conditions, returned to him.

Rampersad has been on remand since late May after being charged with making off without payment. He pleaded not guilty to the charge.

Police previously confirmed that Rampersad was intercepted at the Philip Goldson International Airport on May 29 as he allegedly attempted to leave Belize after Golden Bay Hotel reported that he had departed without settling his bill. Public reporting at the time placed the outstanding amount at $11,470.24 following an approximately month-long stay at the Belize City hotel.

According to the allegations, Rampersad had booked a double room using a credit card, but attempts to process payment were unsuccessful. Hotel management alleged that he subsequently requested several extensions to his stay before leaving the property without making payment. Police later obtained statements, billing records and surveillance footage during their investigation.

Rampersad was later offered the possibility of bail subject to strict conditions, including securing a Belizean surety and confirming prepaid accommodation in Belize. He remained behind bars after failing to satisfy all of those requirements.

He is scheduled to return to court on August 28 for confirmation that the terms of the mediation agreement have been met.

World.title: Ryan Herbert gets six months for 0.6 grams of crack cocaine; his 13th conviction
World.content:
Ryan Herbert gets six months for 0.6 grams of crack cocaine; his 13th conviction

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City mechanic with a lengthy record of drug-related convictions was sentenced to six months in prison on Thursday after pleading guilty to possession of 0.6 grams of crack cocaine.

Ryan Harold Herbert, 27, of Peter Secco Street, appeared unrepresented before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he changed his previous not guilty plea to guilty.

Herbert reportedly expected to receive a fine, but the court took into consideration his extensive criminal record. With Thursday’s conviction, Herbert now has 13 previous convictions, including nine for drug-related offences and four for traffic offences. It was also his third drug conviction for 2026.

The Chief Magistrate consequently imposed a custodial sentence of six months rather than a fine.

The charge stems from an incident on May 21, 2026, when members of the Eastern Division Operations Team were conducting patrols on Flamboyant Street in Belize City.

Police reportedly observed a group of men gathered in a yard during a period when portions of Belize City were under a state of emergency. Officers stopped to conduct searches for illegal drugs, firearms and ammunition.

During a search of Herbert, police allegedly found small, cream-coloured substances in his right front pocket that were suspected to be crack cocaine. The substance was later weighed at 0.6 grams.

Herbert was arrested and charged with possession of a controlled drug. He initially pleaded not guilty but changed his plea when he returned to court on Thursday.

Herbert has since been taken to the Belize Central Prison to begin serving his six-month sentence.

World.title: Frank Young remanded back to prison after 9-year-old girl alleges that not only did he sexually assault her; he forced her to perform oral sex for $50 – secret she kept for over a year
World.content:
Frank Young remanded back to prison after 9-year-old girl alleges that not only did he sexually assault her; he forced her to perform oral sex for $50 – secret she kept for over a year

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 21-year-old construction worker from Lords Bank Village, Ladyville, has been hit with a second count of sexual assault and sent back to prison after new allegations surfaced during a recent bail revocation proceeding.

Frank William Young appeared before Chief Magistrate Deborah Rogers in Court #1 on Thursday afternoon at around 12:23 p.m., where he was formally read the additional charge in the presence of his attorney, Javier Williams.

The initial incident dates back to July 5, 2025. According to the original police report filed on July 9, 2025, the 9-year-old victim asked Young—her older cousin’s boyfriend—for money to go to the store. Young gave her a $10 bill and instructed her to take $1.00 for herself and $1.00 for another child, and to bring back the change. When the minor walked home around 7:00 p.m., Young allegedly ran toward her near her gate, grabbed her around the neck, squeezed her right buttock, and demanded to touch her private parts in exchange for keeping the change. Following a struggle where she received scratches to her neck, the child escaped and alerted her family. Young was subsequently arrested and arraigned later that month on charges of sexual assault and harm.

The case took a major turn on Friday, August 14, 2026, when the victim was summoned to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court for Young’s bail revocation hearing. Before giving testimony, the child spoke with a court counselor and revealed critical details omitted from her original report.

She disclosed that during the same July 5, 2025 encounter, Young did not only allegedly grab her buttocks, but pulled down his pants and forced her to perform oral sex on him. She reported that Young then gave her $50.00 before she managed to escape to her father’s residence. The child stated she had kept these details secret for over a year due to fear.

Following the disclosure, police reopened the investigation. On Tuesday, August 18, 2026, Young visited Precinct 2 Police Station where he was detained. After an official interview conducted in the presence of a Justice of the Peace, he was formally re-arrested and charged.

During today’s court appearance, Chief Magistrate Rogers took no plea from Young, as additional disclosure must be provided to the defense given the new charge stemming from the same event. The Chief Magistrate informed Attorney Williams that the complete case file has been forwarded back to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) for further directives.

Bail was denied, and Young was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 30, 2026. Defense Attorney Williams indicated that he will be applying to the High Court for bail on behalf of his client. Williams also publicly questioned the delay in disclosure, noting it was unusual for such a critical aspect of the allegation to be brought forward more than a year after the alleged incident.

World.title: The silent thief is robbing young Belize, here is what to own so it cannot
World.content:
The silent thief is robbing young Belize, here is what to own so it cannot

By Horace Palacio: There is a thief working every district of this country, and he has never once been arrested.

He does not climb through windows. He walks straight through the front door of your bank account. His name is inflation, and his method is elegant. He never takes your dollars. He drains what your dollars can do.

The hundred dollars under your mattress still says one hundred next year. But watch it at the counter. The rice costs more. The rent costs more. The bus, the chicken, the cement, all quietly up. Same bill, smaller life. And because Belize imports nearly everything, as this column has hammered all year, we import our inflation too. Every price rise in America and China ships here inside the container, and our pegged dollar carries it faithfully to your till.

Now here is the trap most young Belizeans are standing in right now. You were taught that the responsible thing is to save. Put it in the bank. Watch it grow. But look honestly at what the bank pays on savings, next to nothing, while the cost of living climbs past it year after year. Saving cash alone is not safety. It is losing slowly, politely, with a passbook.

So let me give you the one rule that separates the people inflation robs from the people inflation cannot touch.

You cannot save your way past inflation. You can only own your way past it.

Because the thief has one weakness. He can only steal from cash and wages. He cannot steal from things. When prices rise, the man holding only dollars gets poorer, but the woman holding land, skills, animals, and a business watches her holdings rise with the very tide that drowns him. The wealthy are not outrunning inflation because they are smarter. They are outrunning it because they own. I have preached ownership in this column for a year. Today, the practical edition, for the young Belizean starting with little.

One caveat first, because honesty is the house rule here. I am a columnist, not your licensed financial advisor, and nothing here is a promise of returns. These are principles, ranked for the young and the broke, starting with the asset that costs almost nothing.

Asset one. Your skill. The most inflation-proof asset on planet earth sits between your ears. A certified electrician, a skilled welder, a sharp bookkeeper, a young person fluent in the digital tools I keep writing about, these people reprice themselves as prices rise. A wage is fixed. A skill negotiates. And in the age of AI now circling our job market, the premium on skills machines cannot fake is climbing monthly. Free courses, cheap certifications, a trade learned beside an older master, this asset starts at zero dollars and compounds for fifty years. Buy it first. Buy it always.

Asset two. Land. Your grandfather knew this without a single economics class. Land is the classic Belizean shield, because they are not making any more of it, and because, as I wrote in the home ownership series, our land is being discovered by wallets far heavier than ours. Every year you wait, the gate price rises. So buy small, buy far, buy early, the modest lot on the edge of the village today is the family foundation of 2040. And hear the caution that protects you, verify every title at the Lands Department before a dollar moves, insist on proper transfer, walk the boundaries yourself. Land fraud is real, and diligence is the fence around this asset. But done right, understand the contrast that changes lives. The car loses value the moment you drive it off the lot. The land gains value while you sleep. Land before car. Always land before car.

Asset three. Credit union shares. The institution three Belizean women started with seventy five cents now anchors a movement holding over a billion dollars, and it pays its member-owners dividends, typically well above what a savings account whispers. Start with the minimum. Feed it every payday like a bill you owe yourself. And here is the double power, your growing shares become the borrowing strength that later buys the land and the tools. The credit union is the young Belizean’s on-ramp to everything else on this list.

Asset four. Things that earn. Now we reach the difference between looking rich and getting rich. The poor buy things that cost money and call them assets, the rims, the newest phone, the upgraded car. The builders buy things that make money. The deep freezer that sells cold drinks by the school. The sewing machine filling uniform orders. The mower, the drone, the tools of a weekend trade. And notice the inflation magic, a business can raise its prices when costs rise. A salary cannot. Owning even a tiny business puts you on the collecting side of inflation instead of the paying side.

Asset five. Things that grow. This is the oldest Belizean wealth of all, and it is roaring back. I reported this year how our cattle industry exploded into a formal export trade worth tens of millions, with Mexico asking for every certified head we can send. A weaned calf, my friends, is a savings account that eats grass and gains weight. Chickens, honey, cacao, plantain on that lot you bought, agriculture pairs your land with your labor and pays you in the one commodity whose price never stops mattering, food. In an import-addicted nation, the young Belizean who produces food holds an asset with a permanent customer.

Now the honest paragraph, because some of you are already typing the question. What about crypto, what about the schemes flying around WhatsApp promising to double money in weeks? Hear me plainly. Anything promising quick doubling is a pyramid wearing makeup, and Belize has buried enough savings in those graves. As for crypto itself, it is a speculation, violently up, violently down, and a lottery ticket is not a foundation. If you must touch it, touch it last, with only money whose loss would not bruise you, after the skill, the land, the shares, and the earning assets are in place. Foundations first. Casinos never.

And the discipline that powers all five, pay yourself first. Ten percent off the top of every paycheck, invisible, automatic, before the phone company and the weekend see it. Small money into real assets, every month, without drama. Then multiply it the way our people always have, by pooling, the family land bought together, the partner savings circle with people you trust and rules in writing, the syndicate of three friends buying the lot none could afford alone. I wrote it in the ownership series and it remains true, what is impossible alone is routine together.

So here is the whole article in one breath, young Belize.

Inflation is a tax collected only from the asset-less. Every year you hold nothing but cash and a wage, you pay it in full. The umbrella is ownership, of skill, of land, of shares, of tools, of things that grow, built small, built early, built boringly, every single month.

Your great-grandparents bought land with small money and long patience, and you are living off that decision today.

Somebody in 2075 is waiting on yours.

Be the ancestor.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: André Bauer is US Ambassador-designate to Belize
World.content:
André Bauer is US Ambassador-designate to Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The United States Embassy has announced that André Bauer has been sworn in as the new US Ambassador-designate to Belize.

Bauer is a former South Carolina legislator and served two terms as the state’s lieutenant governor.

In its announcement, the Embassy said Bauer brings a deep commitment to public service, entrepreneurship and American values to the role, and that he will work on advancing Administration priorities.

The Embassy said Bauer and his family are looking forward to arriving in Belize, travelling across the country, and meeting Belizeans.

“Follow along as Ambassador Bauer gets to work and begins building connections across The Jewel,” the statement reads. “We’re just getting started.”

No arrival date has been announced.

The post has been closely watched given the range of shared interests between the two countries, including trade, security cooperation, immigration and development assistance.

World.title: New Digital Platform to provide data on 194 Belizean communities
World.content:
New Digital Platform to provide data on 194 Belizean communities

By Zoila Palma: The International Organization for Migration (IOM), in partnership with the Ministry of Rural Transformation, has launched the Community Profile Information System (CPIS), a new digital platform designed to collect, store and analyze critical information from 194 communities across Belize.

The platform was developed from an IOM-led pilot survey conducted in 2023, which gathered socioeconomic and demographic data from 20 rural communities in southern Belize.

Building on that initiative, CPIS is being funded by the IOM through the Government of the United States to make reliable community information more accessible to decision-makers, development partners and local stakeholders.

The system is expected to strengthen evidence-based planning and improve service delivery by providing timely information on community needs, resources and opportunities. It will also enhance access to community and business data, supporting more targeted and inclusive development programs across the country.

The IOM said CPIS will give stakeholders a stronger information base for identifying priorities and designing interventions that respond to the realities of Belizean communities.

The platform is available online at communityprofile.ruraltransformation.gov.bz.

World.title: Man busted with three bullets has until Friday to decide if he will accept 1-year-4-month sentence or plead not guilty and face trial; Complains he is being kept ‘in the hole’ in jail and doesn’t like it
World.content:
Man busted with three bullets has until Friday to decide if he will accept 1-year-4-month sentence or plead not guilty and face trial; Complains he is being kept ‘in the hole’ in jail and doesn’t like it

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Justin Stephen Goff, 38, who was charged earlier this year after police allegedly found him with three live rounds of ammunition, is considering changing his not guilty plea after receiving a sentencing indication from the Magistrate’s Court.

Goff appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in Court #3, where he sought an indication of the sentence he could receive if he pleaded guilty to keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

The Magistrate informed Goff that a fine would not be considered and that he would instead face a custodial sentence. After taking into account aggravating and mitigating factors, as well as a one-third reduction for an early guilty plea, the court indicated that Goff could receive a sentence of approximately one year and four months in prison.

Goff was given until Friday, August 21, to decide whether to accept the sentencing indication and change his plea or proceed to trial.

During the hearing, Goff complained about his current prison conditions, telling the court that, as a repeat offender, he has been kept in “the hole” since returning to prison in April.

“That’s not a place I like to be,” Goff told the court.

Goff was first arraigned on April 7, 2026, and pleaded not guilty to keeping unlicensed ammunition. Police allege that on April 3 he was found with three live rounds — two S&B-brand rounds and one Aguila-brand round.

At his arraignment, Goff denied the allegation and claimed that the ammunition had been planted on him by the same police officer who later arrested and charged him.

Goff is expected back in court on Friday, when he must indicate whether he will accept the proposed sentence and plead guilty or continue with his case to trial.

World.title: How Dis Mek? Raft built to last, made to enjoy Jamaica
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — River rafting is a popular vacation activity for locals and visitors in Jamaica, but have you ever considered the mechanics behind the raft?

In the latest episode of the Jamaica Observer’s How Dis Mek?, Captain Claude Johnson of Rafting on the Martha Brae explains the manufacturing process behind the structure that drives one of the island’s most recognisable leisure activities.

Each joint on a stalk is essentially an air-filled sealed vacuum, allowing the stalks to float extremely well. If some joints pop open, due to age or sun damage, as long as the others remain sealed, the integrity of the raft is maintained, Johnson explained.

To create the raft, captains need a ‘dozen’ stalks, which for rafting means 14, at a cost of $10,000, tied together with metal wire.

Tune it to an all-new How Dis Mek? on all Observer platforms.

World.title: Assault on tax dodgers!
World.content:
Owners of 432 delinquent properties in the Half-Way-Tree area are about to come under closer scrutiny as the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) and Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) take their tax compliance campaign into the busy commercial district today in pursuit of $162 million in unpaid property taxes.

The three-day field operation forms part of the third phase of an 11-month joint revenue drive aimed at improving compliance and recovering outstanding property taxes, trade licence fees, and signs-and-billboards obligations.

The campaign follows an intelligence-gathering exercise in which the two agencies compiled information on property owners, businesses, trade licences, and other commercial obligations in the Half-Way-Tree area.

Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby said the information gathered has revealed the extent of the problem, with some property tax arrears stretching back many years.

“Excluding the current financial year 2026-2027, there are 432 properties in the Half-Way-Tree area with property tax arrears going back six years totalling $162 million. Of those 432 properties, 151 are associated with businesses accounting for $96 million of that total. On the trade licence side, 195 businesses are registered in this category in the selected area with estimated arrears of $48 million,” he said, during a press conference on Tuesday.

According to the mayor, the operation is intended to improve compliance while ensuring that businesses meet their statutory obligation to pay taxes and fees.

“Let me be clear about the tone and intent of this initiative: This is not an exercise in harassment. It’s an exercise in fairness and accountability. Every one of us has a statutory obligation to pay our taxes, and we intend to see that obligation met. When legitimate business owners pay their fair share, it is unfair for the others operating alongside them to benefit from the same public infrastructure, road rehabilitation, street lighting, public sanitation, drain cleaning, and municipal park maintenance, without contributing to its upkeep,” he noted.

Over the next three days, field teams will be visiting businesses and providing information and guidance to operators on how to bring their accounts up to date.

The area has been divided into three zones to facilitate the exercise.

Zone One covers Hagley Park, Eastwood Park Road, Red Hills Road, Westminster Road, Lower Sandringham Avenue, and Woodglen Drive.

Zone Two includes Hope Road North, Surbiton Road, Waterloo Avenue, West King’s House Road, Constant Spring Road, North Avenue, Central Avenue, South Avenue, Merrick Avenue, Ellesmere Road, Suthermere Road, and North Odeon Avenue.

Zone Three covers Half-Way-Tree Road, Balmoral Avenue, Maxfield Avenue, Hagley Park, Hope Road South, Winchester Road, Ruthven Road, Skibo Avenue, Bradley Avenue, Ballater Avenue, Cargill Avenue, Cecelio Avenue, Stratham Avenue and Clock Tower Plaza Road.

Rather than simply asking delinquent operators to report to municipal offices, the agencies are taking services directly into the commercial area.

A temporary customer service desk will operate at Constant Spring Arcade from 10:30 am to 2:00 pm each day during the three-day exercise. Property owners and business operators will be able to get help registering for online payments, obtain printed copies of official trade licences, settle payments, regularise signs and billboards approvals, and resolve account queries.

The approach is intended to make it easier for businesses to address outstanding obligations while giving them an opportunity to get clarification and assistance without travelling to central municipal offices.

TAJ Deputy Commissioner General for Operations Dave Jeffrey said the Half-Way-Tree operation builds on similar joint exercises the agency has carried out with municipalities in St James, Portmore and St Catherine.

He said those operations had produced significant improvements in compliance, with some areas moving from rates as low as 25 per cent to as high as 75 per cent by the end of the intervention.

Jeffrey said the agencies are aiming for an even stronger result in Half-Way-Tree.

“For this operation, we have expanded our focus beyond property tax to include trade and business licences and the signs and billboards. The operation covers an 11-month period and is slated to end in March 2027, and by that time, we’re aiming that the collection rate will go up to at least 85 per cent of the outstanding property taxes and trade and business licences arrears,” he said.

The three-day outreach is not the end of the campaign. It is part of a four-phase process that will move from planning and intelligence-gathering to direct interaction with taxpayers and, ultimately, enforcement.

According to Jeffrey, the agencies are deliberately trying to change the way businesses approach tax payments by encouraging them to use online services.

“For the interactive session, we are encouraging business operators to make their payments online. As a result, we will not be having a mobile bus for the interactive session. These are business and commercial entities, and we really want them to utilise the online payment and hence why we won’t be having the mobile unit… We want to change that culture and that habit of tax payment and we’ll be doing everything to facilitate that process,” he said.

During the interactive phase, TAJ will serve notices, provide support to taxpayers, facilitate online queries, and engage directly with businesses to help them address outstanding obligations. Compliant taxpayers will also be recognised with congratulatory certificates as part of the initiative.

World.title: No more moos
World.content:
Moo Moo was injured in a hit and run along Walks Road in Spanish Town, St Catherine. Naphtali Junior

AFTER days lying in the sun as residents did their best to provide the care she needed, Moo Moo’s story has come to a heartbreaking end.

The injured cow, who captured the hearts of residents on Walks Road in Spanish Town, was euthanised by the Veterinary Services Division on Wednesday after the professionals determined her injuries were too severe.

Reports are that the cow was injured in a hit-and-run incident on August 11. Residents said they made several reports and calls to animal-related facilities, but were unable to get assistance for the animal. Gabriel Hamilton and Nicholas Thomas became the beloved animal’s primary caregivers, staying with her until her final moments.

The animal’s owner has not come forward.

Dr Sophia Ramlal, director of veterinary services in the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, confirmed that the cow was euthanised using chemicals on Wednesday at approximately 10:15 am after examinations revealed that her injuries were significant and she could not be treated back to health.

“We could determine from the physical examination that both her right front leg and her right hind leg were broken. She was therefore unable to stand and unable to walk around. It is my information that this accident occurred approximately one week ago. However, the ministry became aware of this yesterday (Tuesday),” said Ramlal.

She added that a physical examination could not confirm the cow was pregnant, given its position on the ground.

Ramlal said the euthanasia was conducted by a team comprising members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), the Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA), and the National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA). She said the actions were carried out in keeping with provisions under the Cruelty to Animals Act.

“Provided that the JCF is advised by either a justice of the peace or a registered veterinarian that the injuries that the animal has suffered, in this case a cow, are so severe that the animal should be put to sleep, then that process can occur,” she explained.

“We wanted it to be done humanely. We wanted to make sure that we dealt with it as professionally and expeditiously as we could, and her carcass was moved right after she was put down,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Responding to comments on social media requesting that the cow be harvested for beef, Ramlal explained that because chemicals were used, Moo Moo’s remains are not fit for consumption.

“The intent is not for this cow to be salvaged for meat because, given the extent of the injury, [her] health status… is generally unknown. There could be a generic sepsis, and it could be that the meat is not what we consider healthy for eating, so this cow was disposed of and is not safe for consumption,” she said.

Nicholas Thomas said he was saddened by Moo Moo’s passing, but happy she is now pain-free.

“I can’t explain the feeling. I just have to focus on the bright side. Now I can get more sleep, and I just have to try not to cry when I go out there. Sometimes I was up with her all night, around 10 or 11 o’clock, giving her water and just making sure she was alright until morning. I’m gonna miss her,” said Thomas about his beloved Moo Moo.

He was among residents who thought the cow looked pregnant and he had hoped any calves she had could be saved.

“It hurt me, but the bright side is that she’s resting now,” Thomas told the Observer.

Though heartbroken that Moo Moo did not make it, Moo Moo’s other caregiver Hamilton agreed that the actions of the veterinary division was the most humane outcome as it relieved the cow from suffering.

“When I was reaching out for help initially, I knew that this would probably be one of the interventions, but that would be determined by a veterinarian’s assessment. To not see her suffering anymore, a piece of my heart is happy with it, but it’s a life lost, so it’s never a happy day. I know in general Jamaicans don’t look at it that way; they more look at her as livestock, something to eat, or raise. But with animals, when you’re going to eat them, you kill them before you eat them so they are not suffering,” she stressed.

“I don’t like to see animals suffering. I’m just hoping that this will bring awareness to Jamaican people that while they are roaming on the road, we must be the ones to look out for them. It’s not the other way around. I think humans don’t really know how to co-exist with animals and that’s an issue,” she added.

Stressing the need for better treatment of animals, Hamilton extended thanks to the vet services division, Thomas, and other residents who assisted in Moo Moo’s care before her sad end.

World.title: Brighter Days ahead For Romieikon
World.content:
.

Dancehall fusion producer and artiste Romieikon has teamed up with a slew of multifaceted artists for his most recent project, the Brighter Days’ rhythm.

Over the years, Romieikon has released multiple projects under his Britishlinkz imprint that have gained international acclaim through his distinctive marketing modules. He therefore has high expectations for Brighter Days’ rhythm.

Featured on the rhythm are Knaxx (My Life), AI Milly (No Regret), Varian Di-Best (Feel Alive), and Kacique with the title track, each appealing to a different demographic while adding to its international appeal.

Speaking with Romieikon, he shared what inspired the project.

“I always aim to start the year with a positive, motivational note and, ironically, a few months prior to the January 1, 2026 release Hurricane Melissa had devastated the island and the project became my way of motivating the citizens during a hard time that they continue to face,” he shared.

The complete project made its way to digital stores on July 24, with each track amassing thousands of YouTube streams. Subsequently, Varian Di Best’s single made its way to The Beatport’s Reggae Top 100 Chart, where it peaked at #39 while still maintaining a position on the chart.

Kacique, who has worked on multiple projects with Romieikon shares how consistency plays a part in their success thus far.

“We’ve accomplished a lot together, but we’re only getting started. There are even bigger things in the pipeline and I’m excited for what’s ahead,” he said.

He added: “Brighter Days is probably one of my favourite projects because it’s deeply personal. It reflects not only my journey in music, but my journey through life…trusting the process, and having the patience to keep moving forward even when the road gets difficult.”

The Brighter Days project showcases the significance of innovation in music, as well as marketing strategies. With the compilation’s cross-genre appeal, this rhythm is aimed at further solidifying Romieikon’s presence on the scene.

“This is a lifetime project, the marketing of this project will continue even after it has gained recognition. I have pitched the album to all major DSPs, I have social campaigns that will be launched throughout August, I have a campaign specifically for radio and street disc jocks, among other schematics. I expect this compilation to hit more milestones before the end of the year with the continued support of my team and fans,” Romieikon commented.

World.title: HEART in high schools
World.content:
HARRISON… wants it mandatory for high school graduates to have skills certification

MOUNTAIN SPRING BAY, Trelawny — Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon says she will be pushing to have the skills-focused HEART/NSTA Trust programme, now restricted to participants over 17 years old, more deeply integrated into high schools across the country. She has asked teachers for their support as the strategic shift is made.

“I will be working to change that legislation so that we can have HEART working more in the schools, and therefore we can get more support for TVET (technical and vocational education and training) in our schools,” revealed Morris Dixon on Wednesday.

“That’s a big change! So when I do it I want to hear you supporting me in public that this is something that is important for our schools,” the education minister cajoled, Wednesday, while addressing the final day of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association’s (JTA) 62nd Annual Conference which was held over three days at Ocean Coral Spring resort in Trelawny.

Established by late former prime minister and Jamaica Labour Party Leader Edward Seaga in 1982, HEART’s mandate was to provide the country’s workers with the skills needed to boost productivity. Traditionally there have been clear lines drawn between academic and vocational studies, with the latter often regarded as a second option. In recent years, however, there has been a push to change that perception, and it is an issue Morris Dixon has spoken of in the past.

“With all the changes happening globally, TVET is the area that is going to take the world forward. That’s where we’re going to have jobs. And that’s where I need your help with telling parents that your child wanting to be a plumber is a good thing. I want you to be able to tell your parents that if your child wants to do construction, that’s great,” she said Wednesday.

The minister highlighted a global shortage of skilled practitioners, including construction workers, plumbers, and electricians.

“TVET has to be more centrally integrated, even in traditional high schools. It has to be, and you and I agree on this one,” she said to the more than 250 educators in attendance.

Beyond students leaving high school with Caribbean Examinations Council and City and Guilds qualifications, Morris Dixon said it is equally critical for them to be armed with certification in a specialised skill area.

“That’s a fundamental change in the system, but it’s something that I’m committed to working with, and I hear the [JTA] president is also interested in that area,” said the minister.

“That is something I’ll be coming back to the JTA on, to help me in championing that change in our system, because it’s important that we have more skills certification in our high schools,” Morris Dixon added.

It may not be a hard sell as JTA President LaSonja Harrison made similar comments during her investiture ceremony Monday night.

“Isn’t it high time that all children leaving high school do so with certification in a skilled area? If we mean our population any good, that needs to become mandatory,” said Harrison.

She also suggested that Government reallocate a portion of the revenue earned from the three per cent payroll tax on businesses, the HEART Trust levy, to assist with upgrading and maintaining technical and vocational schools.

“This only makes sense, to my mind, because these institutions — oftentimes in collaboration with HEART — ensure their students graduate with said certification. I am not just questioning the Government, I’m positing possible solutions as well,” the JTA head said Monday.

“Another option is [that] the monies allocated to provide AI chatbots, via Jamaica Learning Assist, can and should be rerouted to support this,” Harrison added.

World.title: TRUSTING THE PROCESS
World.content:
The Jamaica Kingsmen take a victory lap after their final CPL game at Sabina Park on Tuesday in which they defeated St Kitts and Nevis Patriots by 51 runs. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Keemo Paul says the Jamaica Kingsmen never lost confidence, and on Tuesday night at Sabina Park he proved why.

The all-rounder smashed a half-century and took three wickets to lead Jamaica to a 51-run win over St Kitts and Nevis Patriots — a result that lifted the Kingsmen to back-to-back wins after an 0-3 start and sent them to St Lucia on Friday with momentum.

Paul credited the turnaround to belief in the group and the energy from home fans.

“Well, first of all, the last two games have been perfect for us. We lost three, but we never lost confidence. The crowd has been behind us all the time. They’ve been supporting, and they’ve been driving us. So coming into this game, our confidence was high,” he said.

“We wanted to win. We obviously didn’t want to bat first, but we had to. We got some runs on the board, and in the end we came out victorious. So now we’re two on the trot, and we want to continue this momentum.”

Sent in to bat, the Kingsmen were in trouble immediately. They were 0 for 2 inside the first over and later 54 for 4 in 7.2 overs after Saurabh Netravalkar and Wanindu Hasaranga ripped through the top order.

That’s when Paul and captain Rovman Powell took over.

Paul survived an lbw review early in his knock, then cut loose. He hammered 65 from 36 balls with five sixes and six fours. Powell played the perfect foil with 49 from 39 balls, including four fours and three sixes.

Their 99-run stand for the fifth wicket dragged Jamaica to 153 for 5 in 17.3 overs, and set the platform for a big finish. The Kingsmen ended on 181 for 6.

Netravalkar and Hasaranga both took two wickets for the Patriots, but were expensive. Netravalkar went for 43 from four overs, Hasaranga 36 from four.

“We didn’t get started the way we wanted to. Obviously, it was two down very early. But when I went out there with Rovman he just told me bat some balls. The wicket is not the easiest — our target was to get to 175. We got more than that. So we knew once we got around the range, we were going to be in the game. So I think it was smart cricket, and I’m happy with the win,” Paul said.

“Individually, it [my performance] was good. I mean, I made some runs, but I want to be consistent. It doesn’t stop there. I’m not content with that. I want to contribute to this team. I’m happy in this environment. I’m pleased to be here, and I want to contribute.”

The target proved too much. Paul then turned to the ball and led the fight-back, taking 3 for 30 from his four overs. Andre Russell backed him up with two for 19 from 4 as the Patriots were dismissed for 130 in 18 overs.

Kevin Wickham top-scored for the Patriots with 37, while Navin Bidiasee retired out on 19 and Nikhil Chaudhary added 18. No other batter passed 15 as Jamaica’s bowlers kept the pressure on.

Paul was pleased but not satisfied with his own performance.

“Concerning my bowling, I’ve been working with the Test team, with our bowling coach, Ravi Rampaul, working on my run-up. I’m disappointed with the no-balls. It’s something that I want to correct. So I’m feeling very good.

“I’m hitting the crease good. The ball is coming out really, really good. I just want to stay consistent. Like I said, I don’t want to get complacent. I want to stay consistent, and I want to perform for this team,” Paul affirmed.

Now with two wins on the trot, Paul said the Kingsmen are staying grounded.

“We need more wins. We want to qualify, so we have to play our best cricket going forward, each and every game. We just stay in the moment. Keep our feet on the ground, game by game. We go to St Lucia now, so like I said, we have to play our best cricket each and every match. We can’t get complacent,” he said.

“I mean, Russell and Rovman, they’re the backbone of this set-up, Russell especially. I’ve never played with him, actually. This is my first time. So to actually see him in action is fantastic.

“And everything is okay. I mean, the vibe is great, the atmosphere, the support, our coaching staff has been fantastic, and they have supported us. And once again, I can’t thank the crowd enough.”

World.title: Eggs &…
World.content:
(Photo: Michael Moodie Photography)

For Chef Damion Stewart and Kwasi Henry, the Jamaican owners behind Eggs &…, the idea for the eatery began with travel and a shared appreciation for how something as familiar as breakfast could be reimagined.

Travelling across the world, they shared with Thursday Food, exposed them to breakfast spots that managed to strike an interesting balance: quick and uncomplicated, yet still elevated in taste. A breakfast sandwich “could be convenient without being ordinary, pairing familiar ingredients with unexpected flavours, interesting fixings and thoughtful sides”.

It was an experience they felt was missing back home. That inspiration eventually became Eggs &, a Jamaican-owned concept built around a simple idea: start with eggs, then see where the “&” takes you.

The name is intentionally open-ended. Eggs may be at the heart of the menu, but the ampersand represents everything that can come alongside them different proteins, flavours, textures and combinations that take the breakfast sandwich beyond the expected.

“It also means breakfast doesn’t have to look or taste the same every time,” explained Chef Stewart. It’s no idle boast!

The result is a menu built around local eggs, ranging from $850 to $2,250, that moves easily between the familiar and the unexpected, giving diners a different take on the breakfast sandwich while keeping the experience casual, convenient and accessible throughout the day.

Eggs &… is located on the ground floor of The Rogers Commercial Centre, 56-58 Lady Musgrave Road, Kingston 6, and opens to the public on Monday, August 24, serving its full breakfast menu daily from 7:00 am to 3:00 pm, for dine-in and takeout.
