Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman and elder Lloyd Grimshaw is doing a very specific thing at the parliamentary inquiry into interference at the 2025 federal election: he’s trying to say that the mass participation in the election campaign was all about individual church members acting voluntarily, not the church itself.



So member for Kooyong Monique Ryan asks him specifically, and quotes his “Man of God” Bruce Hales to do so: “Among the writings of Mr Hales is a statement that says that everything you do in your daily life is church business. That being the case, there’s a certain inconsistency here?”

Loading

The quote she’s referring to is one from 2014, when Hales said: “Assembly-minded persons would carry the feature of the house of God everywhere we go. So wherever we are, in any circumstance, in every detail of our lives, we’d be related to the house of God”.



Grimshaw says this should be read in context, “that you know, it’s in your daily life, the church members’ daily life, they’re observed as being part of the Christian faith, and they should act accordingly. So they should act in accord with their Christian faith.”



Following today’s reports about the far-right, Ryan is going through the far-right stunts one by one that she personally was subjected to during the 2025 election campaign and asking Grimshaw to answer whether he knew of any of these people.



“I’d like to ask … whether the brethren has any relationship with or has funded in any way a former member of the Proud Boys by the name of Harrison McLean, who interrupted an asylum seeker resource centre event on the 23rd of April?”

Members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church in Tasmania in 2025.

“It’s the first time I’ve ever heard the name,” he says. McLean has declined to comment to this masthead about his electoral activity.



What about agitator Matt Trihey, she asks – who conducted a stunt in Kooyong? Neo-Nazi Joel Davis? No and no, Grimshaw answers.



She’s also asked about the payments, reported in this masthead this morning, to right-wing agitators to run stunts. Again, Grimshaw dead-bats it using the familiar argument.



“The Brethren, Plymouth Brethren Christian Church never funded one cent to any political cause or party or candidate in the 2025 election.”

World.title: Cancel him? I barely wanted to read about him
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Cancel him? I barely wanted to read about him Robert Moran August 21, 2026 — 12:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before Alex Cooper became Gen-Z’s Oprah and head of the multimillion-dollar Unwell Network, she was hosting her then nascent Call Her Daddy podcast on Barstool Sports, the media platform founded by Dave Portnoy. Portnoy, a former salesman, had turned Barstool Sports from a self-published sports-and-gambling paper – “the only newspaper in Boston written by the common man, for the common man” – into an online empire, a founding pillar of today’s manosphere. In 2018, Cooper and her then partner Sofia Franklyn debuted Call Her Daddy to immediate success, thanks to their unfiltered and polarising discussions about sex. Within weeks, it was the number one podcast on iTunes, making Portnoy’s initial contract with the women – $75,000 per year for three years – awkwardly lowball. In April 2020, as a contract dispute flared, Cooper and Franklyn went silent. Dave Portnoy’s memoir is an act of myth-making and score-settling. Getty Images It’s here, 225 pages into his loathsome memoir, where Portnoy makes what’s surely the most egregious accusation in a book filled with wild claims: he alleges that Cooper told him she and Franklyn planned to falsely claim they were sexually harassed at Barstool Sports if he didn’t let them out of their contract. “In April 2020, you may recall that the world was pretty furious with men and their workplace behaviour toward women,” Portnoy writes. “For years, Barstool and I had been pilloried for making sexist jokes, but we’d never been accused of inappropriate workplace conduct... Even though it was patently untrue, it would have been a tough fight for us to win in the court of public opinion.”



Cooper was willing to accept his new deal, Portnoy writes, while Franklyn – advised by her then-boyfriend Peter Nelson (“Suitman”) – stalled. Sensing discontent between the pair, Portnoy admits he fed information as an “insider” to the New York Post that Cooper and Franklyn hated each other to torpedo any plans they had of taking Call Her Daddy elsewhere. Their partnership collapsed, Cooper finished her contract with Barstool and walked away with Call Her Daddy’s IP, eventually spinning it into a $60 million deal with Spotify and then a $125 million deal with Sirius XM. “I have no f—ing idea what Sofia is doing,” Portnoy gloats. Alex Cooper, host of the Call Her Daddy podcast and founder of the Unwell Network, got her start on Portnoy’s Barstool Sports. Getty Images It’s a wild story, but you can see Portnoy’s reason for telling it. This is memoir as myth-making and score-settling. If we get a fascinating glimpse of the “inside baseball” of new tech along the way, it’s accidental. In the foreword, Portnoy reveals that he only did the book because he was offered a seven-figure advance. To his followers, this kind of stuff reads as cool-guy bravado, another maverick sticking it to lamestream institutions. The rest of us might interpret it as contempt for the reader.



Portnoy puts the “tool” in Barstool. His dimwittery has been the secret to his success – the “Barstool Difference”, he calls it, which is about all the times he’s turned dumb mistakes into an asset, or something. Like during the Boston Marathon bombing, when Barstool’s lack of journalistic standards made it a prime source for breaking news. ”The Barstool logo was splashed across every major news outlet,” Portnoy recalls. “Not only did we have better sources with boots on the ground than traditional media, we had no restrictions on posting stuff. We didn’t have to vet our information like they did. As a result, the local news was at least thirty minutes behind everything we posted… Was it all accurate? No, I definitely had a few pieces of misinformation go out. At one point, I reported that some random kid who had died in the Charles River was a terrorist and was involved with the bombing. Turns out, he had absolutely nothing to do with it. No harm, no foul. He was already dead.“ The “Barstool Difference”: Portnoy is among the most successful figures in the online manosphere. Bloomberg Portnoy is so up himself he should change his nickname from “El Presidente” to “El Colonoscopy”. In this book, he also claims he invented the word “smokeshow” and that the popular gossip site Deuxmoi only exists because of him. Who would even care to fact-check it? Most pages are filled with Portnoy’s petty beefs – with ungrateful ex-employees like Sofia Franklyn and Pat McAfee; “self-proclaimed feminists” who protested Barstool’s “Smokeshow of the Day” pinups and “Blackout” college parties; the journalists at Business Insider who reported on sexual misconduct and assault accusations against him; “serial protesters” like Occupy Wall Street, who “just hate their lives, hate this country, and want somebody to blame for their misery”; woke elites like Zohran Mamdani and Gavin Newsom (“I DESPISE him. And my disgust started during COVID”); and the ex-girlfriend who cheated on him with a SoulCycle instructor.



Besides his ex-wife Renee, one of the few people to get a sweet word is Donald Trump, who Portnoy interviewed in July 2020. “After the interview was over, Trump told me to follow him into a room. No cameras, just the two of us. It was a little closet/gift shop room and he told me, ‘This is the Monica Lewinsky room.’ We both shared a laugh,” Portnoy writes. It’s funny in the same way the “This is fine” meme is funny. Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy spins myths and settles scores in his new memoir. Simon & Schuster Cancel Me If You Can is both the rantings of a little man and a peek into the psychotic entrepreneurial mindset that currently rules both culture and global politics. Beyond Barstool, whose relevancy has sustained through new online personalities like Brianna Chickenfry, Portnoy has 5.7 million followers on Instagram and 4.7 million followers on TikTok, where he posts reviews of pizza like someone gave a phone to the guy who sleeps on the beach. But it’s never enough. “I swear we literally launched a cottage industry of lunatics whose entire career was just to follow what I said and then attack me for clicks,” Portnoy writes of journalists at Deadspin, The Daily Beast, Business Insider, The New York Times and The Washington Post (the “No Fun Squad,” he calls them). “The last thing I was going to do was sit back and be lectured by these hypocritical, entitled douchebags about how awful Barstool Sports was. I was going to attack back, make fun of them, humiliate them. I would make them regret getting into the ring with me,” Portnoy pouts, index fingers slamming down on the laptop keyboard as he lies shirtless on his poolside deck chair.



Welcome to cultural power in 2026. One day we’ll look back and laugh, surely? Cancel Me If You Can by Dave Portnoy is published by Gallery Books. What else is happening in the book world? This is the email many authors dream of getting – but beware, it could be a trap

World.title: Father of Cats star denies he was threatened over debt to Hells Angels as video emerges showing him barking like a dog
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaAFL 2026 Father of Cats star denies he was threatened over debt to Hells Angels as video emerges showing him barking like a dog Cameron Houston and Carla Jaeger August 21, 2026 — 12:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A bankrupt tradesman and the father of Geelong footballer Tanner Bruhn appears to have been forced to say he owes money to the Hells Angels outlaw motorcycle gang while being threatened by an unidentified man. Matthew Bruhn, 51, was ordered to “bark like a dog” as he knelt in a park while dressed only in underpants and a T-shirt, according to a 23-second video obtained by this masthead. Loading It is unclear if Bruhn was threatened with a gun during the ordeal, but he is told to “start barking like a dog, before I put one in you”. The 51-year-old plumber is instructed to identify himself and confirms he owes money to a Hells Angels member, but does not discuss the specifics of the debt.



Matt Bruhn and his son, Tanner, date unknown. However, Bruhn has a different take on the footage, and claims through his lawyer that “the video was made in jest with some friends and was not intended to depict, and should not be represented to be depicting, actual or true events or circumstances”. “That is to say, our client says he does not owe any money to and has not had any dealings with or associations with the Hell’s Angels OMCG,” said solicitor Anthony Murdoch from Patten Robins Lawyers. Police have attempted to speak with Bruhn regarding the video, but he was described as “unco-operative”. “Victoria Police has conducted enquiries regarding the circumstances depicted in the video and assessed all information presently available. Investigations are ongoing at this stage, so it would be inappropriate to make any further comment,” a police spokeswoman said.



Bruhn, who was declared bankrupt for the second time in March 2024, has continued to rack up debts with other tradespeople and clients of his business, Southwest Insurance Maintenance Business. Bruhn was countersued in 2023 following allegations he had defrauded a vulnerable mother of $500,000, leaving her on the brink of homelessness. According to court documents, the mother of five, a domestic violence survivor, met Bruhn in 2021 when he was engaged to provide NDIS-funded care for her disabled children while the family was living in a caravan. Bruhn allegedly preyed on the mother to orchestrate a financial scheme under the guise of renovating her two homes to prepare them for sale. He befriended the mother, allegedly gaining access to her phone, banking details, passwords and other financial documents. According to court filings, Bruhn falsely claimed to be a qualified builder and over a period of two years collected $193,000 from the mother while performing little, if any work on the properties.



Bruhn is also accused of incorporating a business in her name, which he used to secure a $300,000 high-interest, short-term loan against her properties, and diverting the proceeds to himself. Matt Bruhn’s alleged debts Vulnerable mother: Bruhn is accused of defrauding an unemployed mother of five out of $500,000, leaving the woman on the brink of homelessness. Santiago Aznal: Aznal claims he lost $100,000 after Bruhn failed to repair the damaged roof of his Strathmore home. Bellarine Peninsula couple: A couple with two young children say they were left with a $308,000 debt, accusing Bruhn of misleading and deceptive conduct. The mother lost one of her homes in June 2023 after defaulting on loan repayments her lawyers claim she was unable to understand. “[The mother] was a vulnerable person who had little or no financial acumen and was suffering from the effects of domestic violence,” the counter-claim said. “[The mother] has a learning difficulty ... and has significant difficulty with numeracy and financial concepts.” The private lender’s case to repossess the woman’s second home was dismissed after she filed a counterclaim, while Bruhn’s lawyer denied the allegations against his client.



Related Article Courts The dramatic moment that sank the rape case against Geelong midfielder Tanner Bruhn One disgruntled customer, who alleges he advanced $10,000 to Bruhn to repair the damaged roof of his Strathmore home last December, has sent dozens of text messages, emails and legal letters in a futile bid to recoup the money. Santiago Aznal also attempted to have the dispute mediated by the Building and Plumbing Commission, but Bruhn failed to show up. “How do you live with yourself? You were in our home, shook my hand and looked me in the face,” said Aznal in an SMS on February 23. Aznal said Bruhn would constantly refer to his son, Tanner, who was charged with rape and missed an entire AFL season until the case against him collapsed in November last year after a key prosecution witness was found to have lied to police.



Aznal sent a letter to the footballer via the club. “Your father did mention to me that he was Tanner Bruhn’s father and what you and your family had been through last year. I sense now this was simply a tactic employed by your father to gain empathy from us,” he wrote. Matt Bruhn (right) denies allegations of wrongdoing. Bruhn’s lawyer denied his client had ever used his son’s AFL career to further his business interests. “Our client denies ever using his son Tanner Bruhn’s name (Tanner) to establish credibility or obtain work. Our client intends to write to Mr Aznal and ask him to correct all untrue statements he has made,” solicitor Anthony Murdoch said.



However, Murdoch confirmed his client had racked up debts. “Our client concedes that he did owe people money, but not the Hell’s Angels. He further concedes that he became an undischarged bankrupt after his business collapsed, which therefore means his creditors are being lawfully handled by his bankruptcy trustee,” Murdoch said. Bruhn was declared bankrupt again in 2024, after allegedly leaving a couple with a $308,000 debt after he was engaged to repair a property on the Bellarine Peninsula. His company was forced into liquidation in 2023 after Bruhn failed to repay the money, with the couple alleging he had been misleading and deceptive about his licensing and insurance when taking on the project.



Editor's pick Opinion

Victorian election Zero policies and a blank page: Pauline Hanson doesn’t look serious about Victoria Chip Le Grand State political editor Liquidator Neil McLean’s November 2023 report noted that Bruhn’s company’s bank account had a balance of just 71¢, and found Bruhn had breached several director duties. Last year, Bruhn’s photo was shared to a “dodgy builders” Facebook page, with an anonymous post warning local tradies to “beware of this bloke”. Several Facebook users responded alleging they had also been scammed by the father of three. Bruhn, who is estranged from his son, was a champion footballer in the Geelong Football Netball League and was inducted into the Grovedale Tigers’ hall of fame in 2019. World.title: Housing and crime leave voters increasingly unhappy with LNP
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandResolve Political Monitor Housing and crime leave voters increasingly unhappy with LNP Matt Dennien August 21, 2026 — 12:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Housing and crime are the greatest risks for the Crisafulli LNP government as it approaches the halfway point of its first term, with voter sentiment over its efforts in the past year plunging. Just 22 per cent of voters surveyed in the latest Resolve Political Monitor for this masthead rated the government’s work on housing as “good” – down from 31 per cent one year ago. Sentiment on crime fell from 45 to 37 per cent. The two are the only topics where the balance of views leaned negative. Results from the August portion of a two-month polling snapshot come as the government prepares the next controversial tightening of its youth justice bail laws, now earmarked for adults, and remote sentencing.



That broader polling also found voters’ outlook for both the state and themselves had soured over the past year. October will mark the midpoint for Premier David Crisafulli’s four-year term, after a 2024 election in which the LNP campaigned on fixing “crises” across housing, youth crime, cost of living and health. The primary vote for the LNP has remained relatively steady above the 30 per cent mark since election and post-election highs in the mid-40s. Steven Miles’ Labor opposition has languished in the mid-to-high 20s this year. Ascendant support for One Nation at a state level – akin to that federally and across the country, despite the party having no Queensland state MPs and little focus on state issues – had drawn level with Labor before it ebbed.



Miles used his June budget reply to announce new policy pitches in housing and crime, with the opposition this year pushing back on government efforts that go beyond election vows. On housing, Labor has also appeared to echo the LNP’s strategy while in opposition of hosting “town hall” meetings across the state to hear from – and speak to – the public about their concerns. The government has leaned heavily on efforts to boost housing supply through releasing government-owned land to developers and funding supporting infrastructure, and financial help for first-home buyers. A police report in February mapping community sentiment about youth crime through public sources such as social media gave an “extremely negative” score of two out of 10.

World.title: Bankrupt high-flyer’s Kew pub is back on the market, again
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Bankrupt high-flyer’s Kew pub is back on the market, again Nicole Lindsay August 21, 2026 — 12:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain One of the three Melbourne pubs swept up in the spectacular collapse of Jon Adgemis’ pub empire is back on the market again. The Clifton Hotel on Kew Junction was controlled by the former KPMG high-flyer’s Public Hospitality Group. Adgemis collected a portfolio of 22 pubs, most of them in Sydney, before he was forced into bankruptcy last October owing $1.8 billion. The Clifton Hotel in Kew. His affairs and playboy lifestyle came under forensic examination in the Federal Court in Sydney last week following his group’s disastrous implosion.



Last year, receivers listed the Kew hotel for sale at between $7 million and $8 million, but that was when the pub was still operating. It closed last year for maintenance and hasn’t reopened since. Luckily, the two billboards above the roof, leased to 2031, are bringing in some cash. HTL’s Scott Callow, Daniel Ryan and Andrew Jolliffe have the listing but declined to provide a price guide for the pub which is being offered on a freehold or leasehold basis. The venue features an open-plan kitchen with a wood-fired pizza oven, bars, a private boardroom/dining space and an outdoor terrace. It’s across the road from the four-tower project that Orchard Piper and James Packer’s NPACT group are aiming to build on the former Leo’s Fine Food & Wine supermarket site. Plans have been drawn up for a seven-level hotel to be built above the pub, but local laws now allow for up to 12 levels at the junction, so a property developer may be the likeliest buyer.



Records show Adgemis’ Public Hospitality Group paid $6.8 million for the pub in July 2021 and scored a high-profile tenant in Guy Grossi’s Puttanesca Osteria. But that was a short-lived venture. The Vine Hotel in Collingwood. The title shows three mortgages and five caveats over the property. The same number of mortgages and caveats cover another of Adgemis’ pubs, The Vine Hotel in Collingwood. Last year, the shelf company which owned the empty pub in Collingwood appeared to have gone unnoticed by Adgemis’ corporate undertakers. Records show Adgemis’ shell company, The Vine At Collingwood Pty Ltd, which paid $4.75 million in November 2021 for the hotel, was deregistered in May. The hotel must surely be next on the sales list?



Related Article Commercial real estate The price is high. Football legend Dusty Martin cuts another property tie with disgraced manager The pub on the corner of Derby Street at 59 Wellington Street is next to Gurner’s Victoria & Vine apartment project. Sure there’s a fancy health club in there, but a pub downstairs is a no-brainer. Some reports suggest Adgemis was trying to install a George Calombaris restaurant in the pub. Public Hospitality’s third Melbourne venue was the Saint Hotel on Fitzroy Street, St Kilda, which boasted a short-lived Karen Martini restaurant. It sold at auction shortly before Christmas to the Kokoda Group for $8.4 million. Sales of the 22-hotel portfolio have so far yielded about $80 million.



Tidy profit BWP, the listed trust which owns 66 Bunnings Warehouses around Australia, has splashed out $25.5 million on the Sunbury Lifestyle Centre. The vendor, Kinglake, made a tidy profit on the property which it bought just 18 months ago for $19.6 million. The deal reflected a tight yield of 5.2 per cent. The 5554-square-metre centre is on a 12,140 sq m site at 85 Vineyard Road, next door to the local Bunnings. Tenants included The Good Guys, Repco, Total Tools and Petstock. Sunbury Lifestyle Centre has been purchased by BWP Trust.



The move is part of BWP’s strategy to diversify its income from the purely Bunnings stream and gives the trust control over a 4.78-hectare chunk of land. According to BWP’s recently reported annual results, it derives 67 per cent of rental income from Bunnings Warehouses and 16 per cent from standalone LFR centres. About 12 of its portfolio of 82 properties are large-format centres. Colliers agents Tim McIntosh and Will Heffernan, with Stonebridge’s Justin Dowers, Rorey James and Kevin Tong did the deal. The property attracted 13 first-round offers from local and interstate private investors, syndicates and institutional buyers and five second-round bids, McIntosh said. Jewellery shop



The former Kozminsky jewellery shop on Bourke Street, once tipped to be the new home of the Hopetoun Tearooms, is back on the market, vacant. 421 Bourke Street is next door to Cbus Property’s new tower. Built in 1859, the 380 sq m property is on the corner of McKillop Street next door to Cbus Property’s new tower at 435 Bourke Street which will feature two restaurants owned by Chris Lucas. There were grand plans for the Hopetoun Tearooms to occupy the entire three-storey building at 421 Bourke Street, but they never came to fruition. The Bourke Street building last changed hands in 2019 for $7.6 million, when the Bellesis family, which runs auto plastics moulding business Socobell, bought it from the Giannarelli family.



It was the same price the Giannarellis paid in 2017 when the 165-year-old jeweller, Kozminsky, closed after more than 40 years on Bourke Street. The building has been vacant for nearly 10 years. Colliers’ agents Christian Hatzis, Matt Stagg and Ryan Milivojac are running an off-market invitation-only process for the building and expect more than $7 million. Investors and hospitality groups are expected to make a play for the property which is in the heart of a new corporate precinct. Fast food With the fast-food market growing at speed, it’s no surprise investors are hotly pursuing takeaway joints.



Last week, a new flagship Nando’s in Cranbourne North sold for $5.84 million, reflecting a yield of 5.3 per cent. An interstate investor snapped up the new strata outlet which is in Oreana’s WT Business Park, alongside KFC and Zambrero. Stonebridge agent Rorey James, who did the deal with Kevin Tong, said five of their last six buyers in this sector were from interstate. “So many interstate buyers are seeing value in Victoria. They’re taking a long-term view,” James said. Other recent deals include the Mount Waverley Red Rooster which fetched $6.47 million with a 4.84 per cent yield and a KFC in Clayton, which is understood to have sold for a price reflecting a 4.5 per cent yield.



Related Article Commercial real estate Courtrooms, compactor shelves: Art deco former Supreme Court office sells for $25m The Cranbourne outlet is on a large 1141 sq m site with drive-through facilities and returning $309,585 a year in rent. A new 15-year lease has options out to 2060. In Box Hill, an El Jannah charcoal chicken shop sold at auction for $4.55 million on a yield of 5.38 per cent. It’s a bullish result for the 648 sq m shop at 422 Station Street which is south of Box Hill’s CBD near the corner of Canterbury Road. It’s in a small block of strip retail with no drive-through capacity but a long 20-year lease.



Six bidders made a play for the shop, which sold to a local investor. JLL’s Dominic McGrath, Romanor Falconer, and MingXuan Li handled the auction. “We saw traditional fast-food investors competing alongside private buyers making their first acquisition,” Falconer said. New research from Roy Morgan shows 19.2 million Australians (that’s 82.5 per cent of us) ate takeaway food last year – an increase of 6.7 per cent since 2021-22 – with Millennials the biggest consumers. World.title: His movie was a disaster. His movie about making it is a delight
World.content:
Anthony Frith landed his first movie the hard way. By just asking for it.

Anthony Frith feared he might never get to make a feature film. He ended up making two at once.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If Anthony Frith had realised just how easy it was to break into the movie business, he might have started sooner. He’d been aware of The Asylum, the LA-based churn factory best known for Sharknado, since picking up a three-pack of DVDs from The Reject Shop in Adelaide and bingeing the cheap blockbuster knockoffs with a bunch of mates in a single sitting. “I was like, ‘holy crap, this is amazing’,” he says of the triple bill — Triassic World, 30,000 Leagues Under the Sea and I Am Omega. “I just fell in love.” Flash forward a decade to 2023, and Frith decided to take a punt and email David Latt, one of the founders of The Asylum. Ostensibly, saying he had an idea he wanted to discuss; in truth, he wanted to ask if he could direct one of these cheap-and-nasty knockoffs himself. As it happens, such chutzpah was exactly what The Asylum trades on. “It took about three minutes on a Zoom for me to land my deal with them,” says Frith, laughing at the memory. The tyro Australian director wasn’t an obvious choice to helm a feature film, no matter how shameless a rip-off it was. Sure, he had a couple of filmmaking courses under his belt, but other than some mucking-about-with-mates efforts, his screen credits extended to a bunch of corporate promos (including one for his parents’ industrial cleaning business). If he was the next Martin Scorsese, there was little evidence to show it.



Frith, who is now 36, didn’t come to the table entirely empty-handed, though. He was proposing to make a documentary about the making of an Asylum movie too. “It was part of the same conversation, but they weren’t linked,” Frith explains. “I asked for the film first, and they were going to let me do it regardless, and then the documentary came. As far as I know, I’m the first person to get a deal just by asking for it.” Given The Asylum has turned out something like 350 movies, it’s a little surprising no one had pitched a making-of project before. So, how did Latt respond to the idea? “He thought it was hilarious. He’s like, ‘yeah, sure; we’re going to make the film anyway, so you might as well have your documentary’.” Anthony Frith in the prop room at The Asylum. Frith was a quietly spoken fellow, with a wife and a one-year-old at home in a brick-veneer house in Adelaide, when he embarked on the madcap adventure that has given him not one but two directing credits, the feature film The Land That Time Forgot (based on the 1918 novel by Tarzan author Edgar Rice Burroughs, which is in the public domain and royalty-free, and hence exactly the sort of material The Asylum laps up) and Mockbuster, his documentary about the making of that film. But there’s obviously a tenacious streak beneath the mild-mannered facade; to actually make the doc he pitched in that two-for-the-price-of-one Zoom would take another couple of years, as he went through the far more traditional process (in this country) of applying for and securing the finance (Screen Australia was the principal investor) that would enable him to develop and shoot it.



Without the doc to complicate matters, he says, his Hollywood paymasters “would have sent the script, and I would have been on my way immediately. But they held fire for the sake of the doco.” Actually, paymasters is a pretty loose term in the circumstances. As we see in Mockbuster (henceforth the documentary), the total budget for The Land That Time Forgot (which we will rather generously call “the movie”) was about $US73,000 (around $130,000). His fee? About the price of a return airfare to LA. In the documentary, which cost about 10 times as much to make as the movie, Frith flies to Los Angeles twice, first to meet the Asylum team (the meeting in which he pitched his documentary idea was recreated for the camera because, Frith confesses, he forgot to record it, “which was so stupid of me in retrospect”) and then to oversee some additional scenes for the movie. Talk to Me directors Danny (left) and Michael Philippou visited the set and offered some sage advice: just lean into the craziness and get on with it. Umbrella Both times he paid his own way (well, to be more precise, the travel costs for him and his small crew came from the documentary’s budget). The bulk of both productions were shot in and around Adelaide. Not that you’d necessarily know that from the finished movie. As The Land That Time Forgot opens, the camera is flying high above a mountainous and lush tropical island (at a guess, it’s Hawaii) rather than the flat coastal landscape of the South Australian capital. It’s amazing what you can do with a stock footage library. When Frith had his ducks in a row for the documentary, The Asylum told him what he’d be shooting. Production would start in three weeks. He’d get the script in two. No cast or crew or locations were in place, but he should start planning on the basis of the one-page outline with which he flew home from LA. Your time starts … now!



“It’s wild, it’s crazy,” he says of the timeline. “This wasn’t an instance of them letting things slide, that’s just what they do, it’s how they function as a company.” He needed an experienced local producer on board to make it happen, but it was impossible to convince anyone that the gig was real, or doable – especially once they saw the budget. A behind-the-scenes shot from the movie … or maybe the documentary. Umbrella “A lot of people thought the film was a prank, no one really wanted to commit, there were concerns about what it would do for people’s companies and reputations,” he says. “The Asylum was kind of an unknown quantity to a lot of people, so there was a lot of fear around it, and fear of it being this Candid Camera sort of joke.” Making one movie this way would be stressful enough. But Frith was making two at the same time. He tried his best to keep them discrete, but it was a challenge. “I was mic’d up and the documentary crew had in-ear monitors, so I could talk to them but they couldn’t talk to me. I just had to whisper into the wind and hope they heard me.” The film crew knew the doco was being shot, of course. “But I didn’t want people to be like characters or playing it up. I wanted it to feel observational, I wanted to capture that part of it quite realistically.” In truth, though his influences include the mockumentary films of Christopher Guest, there was little need for Frith to contrive anything for the sake of a laugh. Making a move for The Asylum is inherently an exercise in insanity. From the day he got that one-pager to the first time he saw the finished movie on a big screen was, he says, about six weeks. The six-day shoot was intense but, he says, “I’m glad because any more and my brain would have melted into mush”.

World.title: Macy Gray was dumped by her record label while pregnant. Then her career really took off
World.content:
CultureMusicTake 7 Macy Gray was dumped by her record label while pregnant. Then her career really took off Lenny Ann Low August 21, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Macy Gray released I Try, the biggest hit of her three decade-long career, she was 31, a single mother of three children and resigned to another career after a record deal ended four years earlier. Growing up in Canton, Ohio, she was mocked for having a squeaky, high-pitched voice and stayed quiet as a child, barely able to hold a conversation until the of age 10. But singing brought a Grammy Award, 10 studio albums, and an acting career including Spider-Man and Training Day. In 2012 a music critic at The New Yorker described her vocals as “like honey with the stingers left in”. “I understand myself more now,” Macy says. “I understand what being a mum is. I understand what my purpose as an artist is. And I trust my gut.” Grammy Award-winning singer Macy Gray. Giuliano Bekor Worst habit?



Video games. Right now it’s Grand Theft Auto and a basketball one. I’ve been playing video games since I was a kid. I love it because it’s a great way to waste time. It’s nothing about you. You’re not thinking about anything, and it doesn’t matter if you win. The detail of the games is beautiful to look at. In the basketball one, you can see them sweating. It is a colossal waste of time. I’ll think, “Oh, I could have been doing this. I could have done that.” But, it’s fun. What are you gonna do? Greatest fear? Gray says having grandkids is “the best thing ever”. Giuliano Bekor I’ve always been afraid of heights. The other day I was in Los Angeles and there’s lots of hills and I made a wrong turn. I went up this massive hill, and it took me forever to turn around because I was so scared. I just freeze. My whole body stops. I don’t have it with looking out of planes. There’s just clouds. Nothing’s gonna happen. It’s being in open spaces where I literally freeze up. The line that has stayed with you?



Before my father died [stepfather Richard McIntyre, who raised her with her mother, Laura McIntyre], he asked me if he had been a good dad. It’s a moment I’ll never forget. He was very alpha. I never ever saw my dad be anything less than all-on, on-10, Energizer Bunny. He had cancer, so we knew he was passing and, when we were alone, he asked me that. He was crying when he said it. He didn’t say, “Make sure you take care of my car”. He wanted to know if he had done well as a person. I said, “Yeah”. I was kind of choked. My dad taught me everything but that was the biggest lesson he ever taught me. He died in 2009 and always keep that in mind now when I’m making decisions. Biggest regret? Honestly, that I didn’t spend more time with my kids [Gray has three adult children with her former husband, Tracy Hinds] when they were younger. Their dad wasn’t around, and I didn’t realise until years ago that if I was gone and the dad was gone, they wouldn’t really have somebody. My mum and his mum were around, but that was sporadic. I was in my 30s, and I was still partying. You can’t really go back and fix things. You can only go from here. I have a grandchild now. He just turned two. My little baby boy. Having grandkids is the best thing ever, and I didn’t understand that until I had one. Tell us about your turning point... I was playing at a club called The Roxy in LA in 1994. An A&R guy saw me. I got signed, made a record, but I got pregnant again and they dropped me. I wandered around aimlessly for a few years. I went back to live with my mum because me and my husband split up. Then a guy from Universal Publishing got my mother’s number and called me. I was eight months pregnant at the time with my third. I went back to LA, and the turning point was when my first record [On How Life Is] came out in 1999. Things changed drastically. I got really popular. I had money for the first time in my life. I had people around me I wasn’t expecting. I was going to parties with people I was used to seeing on TV. I’d be sitting there and there’s Elton John talking to me, going “Hey, Macy”. I didn’t know what to say. I was just very, very fortunate.



The artwork or song you wish was yours? Related Article Take 7 Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job Redemption Song by Bob Marley & The Wailers. I have sung it, but I didn’t have the same understanding of what he was talking about then as I do now. I feel like I would sing it completely differently. If you could time travel, where would you choose to go?



The future. I can pick a lottery and get the numbers. I could invent something before the person invented it. I could do a whole business out of telling people’s fortunes. But I believe our spirit and our gut knows what’s going to happen. I think we miss those signals sometimes. Macy Gray plays The Arts Centre Melbourne, September 11; Hindley Street Music hall, Adelaide, September 12; Anita’s Theatre, Thirroul, September 16; Wrest Point Entertainment centre, Hobart, September 18; Sydney Coliseum Theatre, Sydney, September 24 and Enmore Theatre Sydney, September 25.

World.title: Fifty shades of … what? The absurd quest to name colours
World.content:
Wander down the paint aisle of any hardware store, and you’ll drown in pastels, from Fair Bianca to Eggshell via Napkin. See the problem? Back in the day, white was white. But not now. Today one painter’s Vanilla is another’s Rice Cake. Today we deal in glosses and mattes, where Dulux’s Little Lamb is Taubmans’ Albatross. It’s madness on a maulstick.

Even back in 1755, Doctor Johnson waves the white flag. Within his pioneering dictionary, Johnson defined pink as “a colour used by painters”. While blue was “one of the seven original colours”, akin to explaining an apple as an enduring snack. Enter Kory Stamper, a US lexicographer who likens colour-defining as the collision of two forces: “the democratic chaos of language and the curated precision of science”.

On colourful language: When did naming colours become so tricky?

True Color (Knopf, 2026) is Stamper’s bid to map this collision. Her subtitle spells it out: “The Strange and Spectacular Quest to Define Colour – from Azure to Zinc Pink”. The book’s focus is the Merriam-Webster Third Edition of 1961, the same anvil-sized Scrabble bible my grandma bequeathed me.

Gone was the luxury of green, say, being equated to a meadow. Far too facile for 1961. This was postwar America after all, the midst of the science age, where the new world welcomed the polio vaccine and fax machine. Colour boffins were recruited to lend the lexicon a vital precision, a market edge. Yet, the rainbow sputtered for years. Physicist Irwin Priest quit before he started, handing the prism to Isaac Godlove, a chemical engineer, who strove to distil colours with words.

World.title: Shane Jones talks up $50m-$100m koi carp policy amid Treaty stoush over Waikato rivers
World.content:
The government is undermining a Treaty settlement and the health of Waikato and Waipā rivers by prioritising its political interests, Waikato-Tainui says.

The major iwi said it was "unacceptable" to pause Plan Change 1 provisions until 2032, that doing so overrides judicial decisions in favour of the government's donors, and would subject the catchment to "another six years of degradation".

But the Resources Minister Shane Jones argues the new planning system would achieve much the same outcomes, and was promising to campaign on spending $50 million to help eradicate koi carp in the area.

Federated Farmers was also hailing the pause, saying it gave farmers "much needed breathing room" while the resource management system was overhauled.

Ministers on Wednesday announced changes to the Natural Environment Bill replacing the Resource Management Act they said would make the system more practical for food and fibre production.

"The changes will remove unnecessary complexity, better reflect real-world farming and horticultural practices, and provide greater certainty for investment and day-to-day operations," RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said.

That included removing resource caps from the environmental limits framework, expanding what counts as "existing use", extending permits for water infrastructure to 35 years, allowing councils to permit or consent activities already causing adverse effects on waterways (so long as those effects will be curbed over time), and shifting from a model of "no net loss" of indigenous biodiversity to "protect significant indigenous biodiversity".

As well as the previously announced removal of Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements, Bishop said the amendments would also include "targeted action on Plan Changes 1 and 2 to provide respective certainty for farmers and growers in the Waikato and Manawatū-Whanganui while the new planning system is put in place".

Plan Change 1 was a set of farming regulations in the Waikato council's Regional Plan designed to protect the rivers by managing nitrogen, phosphorus, sediment and bacteria across the catchments, requiring farmers and landowners to identify and manage environmental risks through Farm Environment plans and other measures.

The Plan Change stems from Te Ture Whaimana o Te Awa o Waikato - the Vision and Strategy for the Waikato River which was negotiated between iwi and the Crown out of the Waikato-Tainui Treaty settlement - and takes precedence over other regional plans and national policy statements.

The Environment Court made a ruling in June directing Waikato Regional Council to make 20 specific changes, but confirming that once those were done the plan would have been finalised.

In a statement issued as New Zealand First's Deputy Leader early last month, Resources Minister Shane Jones said Plan Change 1 "must be paused before it becomes a bureaucratic death sentence for farmers and growers across the region".

"These rules were designed under a planning system the government is already replacing. It is absurd to force Waikato farmers into costly consents, gold-plated farm plans, and layers of compliance just as Parliament is moving to scrap the very framework that created this mess."

He confirmed to RNZ on Friday the RMA changes would put Plan Change 1 on hold until 2032, saying the Treaty settlement for the Waikato River was "not to be deprecated, however food security cannot play second fiddle to any Treaty settlement or any regional council planning initiative".

"Plan 1 was going to terminate veggie growing in Waikato, and New Zealand First will never acquiesce with the termination of food production in Waikato."

He indicated the pause was likely to become indefinite - effectively a scrapping of PC1.

"Sadly, Waikato Regional Council and Tainui spent too long on this Plan 1 indulgence, and now the new regime is going to supersede what may have been a good idea in the days of Helen Clark, but life has passed those days by."

However, he believed the new planning system would achieve much the same ends.

"The new RMA system has got statutory criteria that will allow for Plan 1 to achieve, in a different form, various outcomes ... I think all iwi need to accept that farmers and veggie growers-they've vastly improved their growing systems. Science and technology has significantly improved, but those types of improvements now have to be mediated through a new statutory regime."

Waikato-Tainui chairperson Tukoroirangi Morgan said the pause "puts political interests ahead of the health of the Waikato and Waipā Rivers and undermines Treaty settlement commitments".

Waikato-Tainui chairperson Tukoroirangi Morgan. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

"After 14 years of work by iwi, farmers and growers, councils, industry, environmental and community groups, it is extraordinary that the Government would simply press pause now, when the process has reached its conclusion," he said.

"We know this is election year, but this is bad news for people and organisations who follow the rule of law and in the next breath have the government step in to override judicial directions at the behest of their political donors."

"Our catchments will now be subject to another six years of degradation which is completely and utterly unacceptable."

Waikato Regional Council similarly said it was disappointing the government had not sought its advice or input on the decision, saying the plan change had been developed by a group including sector, industry and community interests in response to government direction and an independent audit from the Auditor-General.

"It is clear those operating lawfully can continue to do so until 2032 when the responsible authority will transition PC1 into the new planning system. It raises questions for the people who have operated unlawfully," chief executive Chris McClay said.

"PC1 has been one of the most significant and complex planning processes undertaken in the Waikato region. It represents almost $30 million of ratepayer investment and many years of scientific analysis, community engagement, hearings and legal processes.

"Water quality is one of the region's most significant environmental concerns, reflecting its importance to community wellbeing, cultural values, recreation and the region's economic resilience. Waikato Regional Council remains committed to working alongside central government, iwi, communities, farmers, growers, industry and other stakeholders to protect and improve the health and wellbeing of the Waikato and Waipā rivers."

Jones urged patience and trust.

"It seems to me at the nub of this issue is that Waikato and Tainui believe they had a deal with the regional council, and this deal they fear is not going to be fully implemented via the RMA.

"My plea to them is just trust that the new regime - which has the blessings of our Parliament - will deliver the vast majority of what they've sought to achieve for well over a decade.

"Nothing trumps the supreme lawmaking power of Parliament, and our Parliament is ushering a new RMA regime in, and that regime will create a new set of legal conditions for food production, which will void and make unnecessary plan one."

He said Bishop had advised the Cabinet that nothing the government was doing violated any Treaty of Waitangi settlement.

Federated Farmers backed the pause, saying it was a "really positive step for Waikato farmers and a direct response to the concerns we've been raising".

"We've been saying for months that it made no sense to force farmers into a new set of rules when the Government is in the middle of overhauling the RMA, freshwater rules and the farm planning system," president Chris Woolerton said.

"Those farmers were staring down a huge amount of uncertainty and compliance cost just to keep doing what they're already doing ... bringing these requirements into line with the national system is a commonsense and pragmatic approach."

Woolerton said Federated Farmers was frustrated the government had not gone further by addressing restrictions on land-use flexibility.

"This is potentially a major issue for vegetable production in the Waikato ... we need farmers to be able to respond when the market needs more vegetables, not have regulations making it harder to change land use."

NZ First to campaign on $50m to $100m for tackling koi carp - Jones

Jones was adamant part of the problem with the rivers' health was koi carp.

"The threat to the Waikato River is as much to do with the koi carp as well as veggie growers and farmers.

"I've been told over many years that the koi carp is an extraordinarily dangerous and destructive pest in the water-based ecosystems of that area, but it's just never attracted enough government capital either towards the council or to the tangata whenua."

He intended to do something about it.

"The thing to also bear in mind and which I'm going to campaign on, I think we should allocate at least $50m to $100m over time - working with Tainui, working with the council - to eradicate as much as possible the main pest in that area ... the koi carp."

"This time round, New Zealand First is going to deliver that type of practical assistance."

World.title: No guarantee shelter can be provided for every rough sleeper - officials
World.content:
Potaka responds to claims policy boosted homelessness Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Weeks before the government is set to give police powers to move on rough sleepers, officials have admitted to RNZ they can't guarantee immediate shelter for anyone on any given night.

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson says she's grateful it's been "formally acknowledged", but is "deeply distressed" that's the reality in the country.

It comes as the largest provider of the most immediate form of shelter tells RNZ it's managing with the resources it has, but demand is "relentless".

In June, it was reported that Ministry of Social Development (MSD) managers had performance measures related to reducing emergency housing numbers. These measures have now been refocused to achieve "sustainable housing".

At the time, the prime minister admitted he did not know there was no night shelter in Auckland for people sleeping rough.

Since then, RNZ has attempted to understand what shelter is available for someone who is sleeping rough.

Over the past month, RNZ sought clarification from both MSD and the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) - which leads the government's overall programme of work to address rough sleeping - to understand where exactly someone is supposed to go if they need shelter immediately.

After multiple requests, RNZ was finally told by MCERT "there is no guarantee that shelter can be provided for every person in every circumstance in every location".

The agency said access to accommodation was dependent on a range of factors such as "an individual's circumstances, location, service capacity, and real-time availability of accommodation and appropriate support", all of which could change quickly it said.

Robinson told RNZ she'd never had it formally acknowledged there was no guarantee, "I am distressed and I am calling for change."

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson. Auckland City Mission

It comes as the government's move on orders legislation, which has received strong opposition, are being progressed ahead of the election.

The law would give police the power to order people as young as 14 to move elsewhere or face a possible jail sentence if they were being disorderly, begging or rough sleeping.

It also comes following reports of rough sleepers dying outdoors overnight, a man found unresponsive in a Cuba Street doorway in Wellington and a woman found unresponsive on New Brighton beach in Christchurch. RNZ understands another rough sleeper died in Auckland in July.

So for those who had nowhere else to go, and may be told to move on, where exactly could they go?

Understanding the current situation

As recently as Sunday, the minister in charge of move on orders, Paul Goldsmith told TVNZ's Q+A there were "resources available and places available for people 24/7".

Emergency housing grants are the government's primary mechanism for providing immediate shelter to people who have "nowhere else to go" and "can't stay where they are".

Housing Minister Chris Bishop said in July emergency housing still existed "because there will always be people facing genuine housing crises".

"But now it's being used as it was always intended: as a temporary last resort."

Housing providers and social services have consistently said the governments tightened emergency housing criteria has resulted in an uptick in homelessness. That concern was raised by RNZ as early as March last year, with Community Housing Aotearoa chief executive Paul Gilberd saying again this week there was a direct link between the two.

The minister in charge of move on orders, Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

As recently as Thursday, Serena Moran - a nurse practitioner and clinic lead at Te Aro Health Centre in Wellington - told RNZ there'd been an increase in rough sleepers she was treating, including people being released from prison with no plans to continue accessing antipsychotic medication.

She said the reality most days was treating patients who may have been assaulted and having nowhere to send them.

"I basically have to say to them, 'I'm sorry, I can't find you anywhere to stay tonight. You'll need to go back to the street. I'll give you pain relief. I'll try and make you feel as comfortable as I can'."

But ministers and MSD have consistently maintained that emergency housing remains available to anyone who meets the criteria and has a "genuine need".

Ministers and MSD have also repeatedly said that people who did not receive emergency housing could have their "needs met in another way", including through other housing pathways.

Other options include:

transitional housing;

social housing; and

immediate access transitional housing

But none of those pathways guaranteed a person sleeping rough today would have somewhere safe to sleep tonight, especially if the limited immediate access transitional housing beds were full. There were only 65 nationwide.

Kāhui Tū Kaha provided the majority of these beds and told RNZ it was managing with the resources it had, but said the demand was "relentless". It also accepted referrals from police and hospitals overnight.

On Thursday evening, it accepted an elderly woman with physical access needs and a 17-year-old who had both been sleeping on the street. It also accepted a woman becoming homeless due to family violence, and a young woman who police wanted separated from a violent partner.

Kāhui Tū Kaha said things were tight but "we're constantly juggling".

Housing minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What shelter is actually available tonight?

Over the past month, RNZ asked MSD and MCERT multiple times what options were available for someone sleeping on the streets to go somewhere that night - more specifically, to get a bed under a roof within 24 hours.

Through various responses and phone calls, RNZ received the following information.

RNZ was told that emergency housing "is not necessarily the best option for rough sleepers" who may have a range of complex needs and require additional support.

MSD noted there were more outreach and support services for rough sleepers announced in June by associate housing minister Tama Potaka, and referenced the additional $14.5 million attached.

"Of those who approach MSD for emergency housing, 89 percent receive either emergency housing, transitional housing, help with a private rental, or hardship assistance."

In response, RNZ asked for figures around the percentage of people who were declined emergency housing and offered "some other form of assistance", specifically actual shelter tonight - noting that someone could not sleep in a food grant, but an official information act request was required, which has since been made.

MSD also outlined that emergency housing was intended as a last resort - despite earlier stating it wasn't the "best option". Its service centre hours were between 8:30am to 5pm Monday to Friday and 9:30am to 5pm on Wednesdays.

It was possible for clients to receive a short-term grant outside of service hours, to "meet immediate housing needs until client can attend the next available appointment", but MSD wasn't able to provide the percentage of calls received outside hours and how many of those were granted without an official information act request, which has since been made.

Where possible MSD would refer people with an urgent housing need to suitable transitional housing or Housing First placements - these were funded by MCERT and generally provided more support than was available to someone in Emergency Housing.

Associate housing minister Tama Potaka. Alyse Wright

MCERT's response clarified the different housing pathways for those in need:

Housing First

This supported people experiencing "chronic homelessness" to access and remain in stable housing. Support was available for as long as needed, but you had to have been sleeping rough for at least 12 months over the past three years to be considered. Those "new" to rough sleeping weren't elegible by definition.

The government announced an additional 300 homes for Housing First in 2025, following the concerns of increased homelessness.

Transitional housing

Transitional Housing offered "short-term, temporary accommodation" for those who may be affected by a change in circumstances. It also provided tailored support. Emergency referrals could generally be accomodated here.

However, MCERT confirmed the total number of contracted transitional housing places had fallen since 2023, that's despite increasing reliance on transitional housing as an alternative to emergency housing.

It said there were around 300 less places contracted in June 2026, compared to November 2023, reflecting the "planned exit of higher-cost motel-based places, as well as routine fluctuations associated with portfolio management", MCERT said.

As well, when existing transitional housing beds were redesignated as "immediate access" beds from December 2025, MCERT did not specify those beds were replaced elsewhere in the system.

Immediate access transitional housing

This is the most immediate option available, where contracted providers could accommodate eligible households without the need to first go through "standard MSD assessment and referral processes".

MCERT confirmed:

there were only 65 immediate access transitional housing beds nationwide;

all 65 were in Auckland;

only 20 were in central Auckland

RNZ then asked one more time, "what shelter is available and can be guaranteed tonight for someone who is sleeping rough?".

World.title: Report warning of high risk to life from Mount Maunganui landslide went unread by officials
World.content:
A report commissioned just seven months before a fatal Mount Maunganui campground landslide says there was a high risk to life - but councillors never read it.

The report, which features in a meeting agenda for August last year, was reportedly not read by those set to attend.

Six people died in the landslide on 22 January as debris came off Mount Maunganui and covered a large area of the campground.

Tauranga City Council has confirmed an agenda prepared for a meeting of Ngā Poutiriao ō Mauao and the Mauao Trust included a rock stability monitoring report.

A spokesperson said while the report was circulated, the meeting was cancelled, so none of the councillors actually read it.

The chief executive's name is on the agenda's cover, but the council said this does not mean he reviewed it either.

The revelation comes two days after an internal investigation by retired High Court Justice Paul Davison found information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left.

Davison found the failure was not the fault of any one person.

World.title: CNMI’s Carol Lee earns US Open main-draw wild card
World.content:
Northern Mariana Islands tennis standout Carol Young Suh Lee is headed to the US Open after earning a main-draw singles wild card into the final Grand Slam tournament of the year.

Lee, 24, clinched the women's US Open Wild Card Challenge after a strong run on the professional circuit, highlighted by qualifying for and winning the WTA 125 tournament in Warsaw, Poland.

She also qualified for and reached the second round of the WTA 250 tournament in Prague during the four-week challenge.

"I am incredibly grateful and excited for the opportunity to compete at the US Open," Lee said.

"Playing in a Grand Slam in New York is very special to me, especially because I represent the Northern Mariana Islands and am also a US citizen."

The Saipan Community School alumna has represented the Northern Mariana Islands throughout her tennis career, and the US Open wild card marks another milestone in her rise through the professional ranks.

Lee said competing on one of tennis' biggest stages will give her another opportunity to measure her progress against high-level competition.

"This is another important step in my career. Competing against high-level players at big tournaments gives me valuable experience and shows me where my game is progressing. I also get to have the opportunity to inspire young athletes as well," she said.

The 2026 US Open Wild Card Challenge began immediately after Wimbledon on 13 July, with a singles main-draw wild card on offer for one American man and one American woman.

The women's challenge ended on 9 August, with the winner determined by the highest cumulative WTA singles ranking points earned from her best three hard-court results over four weeks.

Lee's strong finish put her at the top of the race, ahead of Caroline Dolehide, who finished second with 122 points, and Elvina Kalieva, who was third with 120.

Lee is currently training at the USTA National Campus in Orlando, Florida, with coach Artem Smirnov and agent Juandell Brunner.

She said the focus is on maintaining the intensity of her training while making sure she arrives in New York healthy and ready to compete.

As she prepares for the biggest stage in American tennis, Lee also spoke about the Philippines and the rise of Filipino tennis star Alex Eala, whom she said she admires.

"I really admire Alex and what she's doing. I can relate to her in many ways, especially coming from a smaller place and carrying the support and pride of the people back home with you," Lee said.

"Seeing where she came from and what she has accomplished is really inspiring to me."

Lee said she has also been impressed by the passion Filipino fans have brought to Eala's matches.

"I also think her crowd is amazing. Tennis traditionally has a certain way that fans watch and behave, but her supporters bring so much energy, passion, and culture into the stadium," Lee said.

World.title: Entire health system under pressure from biggest flu outbreak in 10 years - health boss
World.content:
Flu could hit hard for weeks to come Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

The entire health system is under pressure from the biggest flu outbreak in years, the country's health boss says.

Flu-related hospitalisations are at a 10-year high in Auckland, with national infection rates at a four-year high and rising.

Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley told Nine to Noon the hospital system was "very, very busy" but it did not stop there.

"Whether its from health lines which take calls and triage calls, through to primary care, to St John, to our emergency departments, the whole health system is currently under significant pressure," he said.

A national coordination centre set up this week was diverting staff and resources to help where needed most but it was not always easy, he said.

That was exacerbated by a 27 percent increase in Health NZ staff off sick in the past week.

Influenza A was driving the spike, but there was also RSV, cold viruses and some Covid-19 cases circulating, he said.

Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley. Supplied / Te Whatu Ora

Some of the country's emergency department were seeing record numbers of people through, he said.

He had visited three EDs this week.

"It's very, very busy, our staff are doing a very good job but it is quite difficult circumstances," he said.

Bramley said the Winter Plan, worked out before the season hit, is in action.

There were more people working in telehealth services and Health NZ was working with urgent care clinics to try to get them to increase their opening hours and a small percentage of elective procedures were being cancelled, he said.

About 1500 people around the country had turned up to an ED but been redirected to urgent care, he said.

There were extra hospital beds available and 264 extra staff in place, with 64 doing additional duties to support areas most under pressure, he said.

However, some Auckland health workers spoken to by RNZ this week said they had seen very little evidence of extra beds or staff.

Urgent care clinics in Auckland have had waits of 10 hours or more, and some have not been able to open.

Bramley said there has been a delay in the rapid-build wards promised by the government in November to help ease emergency department pressure, that were meant to be opened in the second half of this year.

World.title: South and lower North Island in for a weekend of strong winds and rain
World.content:
For many parts of the country, instructions for the weekend include tying down trampolines and keeping campervans home in preparation for strong winds and rain.

MetService has issued several wind and rain warnings for both the North and South Islands.

Meteorologist Alwyn Bakker said there was a series of fronts moving over the South Island from the southwest and bringing with it heavy rain and wind strength changes.

"Behind that front, kind of on the Sunday, we're getting strong, cold southwesterlies coming through.

"So what we're expecting wind wise, they're going to be very strong."

An orange strong wind warning is in place from very early on Sunday till the afternoon for Tararua District, Wairarapa, Canterbury High Country, Wellington and the Marlborough Sounds and Southland - south of Gore, including Stewart Island.

Dunedin and Clutha were under a yellow strong wind watch.

Bakker said in exposed areas there was a risk of severe westerly gales reaching 120 kilometres an hour - particularly for Southland.

"If you've got any items that can be picked up by strong winds, you should be preparing.

"Tie your trampolines down, that kind of stuff, and there's a risk of damage to trees and power lines and driving might be difficult, especially for campervans."

Bakker said heavy rain was less widespread than strong wind this weekend but still important.

An orange heavy rain warning was in place for the ranges of Buller and Grey Districts from 3pm Saturday till 9am Sunday.

Bakker said 90 to 120 millimetres of rain was expected over that time and thunderstorms were possible on Sunday morning. There was a minimal chance of upgrading to a red warning.

Yellow heavy rain watches were also issued for the headwaters of the Canterbury lakes and rivers and ranges of Westland District. The rain watches had a moderate chance of upgrading to a rain warning.

"Streams and rivers might rise rapidly, there might be surface flooding, there might be slips," Bakker said.

"We recommend before all of that comes through, just check your drains and gutters to make sure they're all clear."

While there are no snow warnings of any type, some snow was possible for higher roads in the South Island.

Bakker said the strong cold south westerlies expected would drag cooler air from the Southern Ocean. However, it was still unclear how well that would line up with the rain.

"Because there's no good whatsoever if you have lots of warm rain and then the cold air comes through afterwards. You won't get snow."

Bakker recommended that people check back again on Saturday for the latest warnings.

As for the upper North Island, it is currently free from any warnings and watches but that doesn't mean clear weather is expected.

"There's going to be a bit of rain for the upper North Island. It doesn't look anywhere near as heavy as it would be for Westland. Winds don't look too strong through there."

While the weekend is not looking good for most of the country, the beginning of next week is looking somewhat brighter.

"It's going to be another absolutely classic, the weekend is horrible and then it kind of goes all right for the work week.

World.title: Model train fans impressed with City Rail Link ahead of first look at Te Waihorotiu
World.content:
Model trains greet passengers at new CRL station First Up Download MP3 4m

Two days before Te Waihorotiu station reveals itself, the station is filled with only the sounds of howling wind and the footsteps of security patrols.

It's in this setting that Andrew Holt from Auckland Märklin Club arrives with his strong team of five.

With three vans full of models between them, there's no time to take a peek at the new platforms.

"Each individual club member makes their own modules and then we collect them all, bring them in, join them all up together, and hope it all works."

The team has to connect 20 modules together, make sure all the electricals are working, and that the eight trains will be able to run on them, all before Saturday.

Holt, the club's president, said their last two public displays at Maungawhau and Karanga-a-Hape stations had been a great success.

"We've actually been a problem. We've caused bottlenecks because everyone stops. They really want to see what we're doing."

A model, no bigger than the size of an standard office desk, depicts an orchard. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

Auckland Märklin Club was formed in 1987 by model train enthusiasts. The name Märklin comes from the German brand of model trains they often use in their displays.

Setting up for display at the central City Rail Link station, it feels like the tale of two rails - both taking years of work and a lot of dedication. And Holt said both had been someone's dream.

"[Model trains are] a great hobby in terms of all the different skills you learn doing it - in construction, using a drill and using a jigsaw and all that, electronics, just planning the whole scene, what you want to make, building your dream."

Eight trains will be running consecutively on the club's tracks this Saturday. But to Holt, the hobby is more than trains.

"You have a train, but the train needs to go somewhere. And one of the special things I've been told is you need a reason for the train to go there, so build a story around it."

In one of Holt's models he tells the story of how a village stationed next to a waterway slowly grew to a city with apartments, police stations and railway stations.

A corridor at Karanga-a-Hape Station. RNZ / Lucy Xia

As a keen modeller of train stations himself, Holt was impressed by the City Rail Link.

"The stations are really cool. My favourite is the Karanga-a-Hape Station. I think it's everyone's favourite. It's just so deep, and when I'm downstairs you all remember Star Wars, and you've got Han and Chewbacca running around there. I mean, Karanga-a-Hape Station reminds me of Star Wars and the corridors - and I'm expecting the stormtroopers to come running around the other way."

Barry Mccullough's work depicts a sandy beach with train track across the top. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

Holt hoped their display would not only draw more interest to the hobby, but also land them a permanent space. For the last 13 years, they had been running the club through various member's homes.

"We don't have a club room, and that's what we're really hoping for, partially out of this, that we show that we are good."

He said the hosting space could benefit in drawing in crowds regularly who take an interest in the trains, or fascinate over the models.

Among the sceneries on display was Barry Mccullough's work. The 78-year-old has been playing with model trains since he was eight.

"Yeah, I made a lot of them. Did you see the nudists?"

He was pointing to a beach with train tracks built overtop. The module took Mccullough and his wife more than 200 hours to create.

"It's a hobby, we do it when we get around to it. There's no such thing as time."

Every detail on the models are handmade. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

In another module was an orchard setting created by McCullough's wife. The space, no bigger than an office desk surface, is filled with 19 miniature lemon trees, 47 orange trees, six trucks and more than 25 workers.

Dennis Whitlock and Andrew Holt from Auckland Marklin Club are busy setting up the train tracks. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

The couple prepared a special something for the last station's 'first look' day.

"One of the security guys here, the guy in head of organising. On Saturdays (at previous station openings) he wears bright green. Well, she's actually modelled him. And tomorrow night we're going to set it on one of the displays and he's going to have to be here to pick out where he wants to put it. He doesn't know yet."

The first look is scheduled for Saturday from 8am to 6pm. Tickets are free, but booking is required.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki probing claims of force being used against youth
World.content:
Oranga Tamariki is investigating whether a worker at a youth justice facility in Canterbury used force against a young person.

The incident is one of three at Te Puna Wai ō Tuhinapo in the last week.

In response to questions from RNZ, Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive of youth justice services and residential care Dean Winter said one incident resulted in two young people being referred to police, and another involved staff responding to a young person who required de-escalation.

"The third involved alleged use of force by a staff member in relation to a young person's behaviour, and we can confirm this is being investigated."

Do you know more? sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Winter said in all instances the wellbeing of those involved was a priority, with medical checks provided where needed.

"Oranga Tamariki provides regular, ongoing training for staff, and residence management provide a range of support for kaimahi involved in incidents, including sharing learnings about the response."

Winter said young people placed within a youth justice residence may have been sentenced by the court due to their offending, or may be remanded in custody while waiting for a court date due to alleged offending.

"This means that the cohort of young people within a residence change frequently, which can alter the dynamics of each unit. Managing these complex dynamics, while supporting the rangatahi, is part of the operational challenge in our residences."

RNZ earlier revealed there had been two other incidents at the facility, near Rolleston, last month.

At the time NUPE union secretary Janice Gemmell told RNZ they were "preventable" and a "real concern".

"The incidents are serious - staff are suffering serious head injuries and other injuries and it is unacceptable.

"NUPE has been aware of ongoing harm to staff and has raised concern and solutions to the highest levels."

Gemmell said there were a series of concerns being raised by members, including concentrations of young people with high and complex needs, low staffing and risk of ongoing harm to staff and young people.

World.title: Swans captain 'deeply shocked' by scandal, denies player rift
World.content:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills have addressed reporters amid the scandal engulfing the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

Dean Cox and Callum Mills addressed the media. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"As a playing group, we fully support the club's decisions on the sanctions handed down."

Mills said the five players would have to address the playing group, but there was no rift among the players.

Cox confirmed he was not in the room at the centre of the scandal, but would not say whether other staff members or players were present.

Both men refused to answer specific questions about what happened in the hotel room, saying they were the subject of a police investigation.

The Swans players and staff observed the press conference from behind the camera. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cox was also pressed on the club's decision to have the five suspended players driven back to Sydney from Melbourne, rather than flown.

"Decisions were made [as to] how we best support our players within the circumstances that happened," he said.

Cox admitted the club's previously acclaimed culture had "taken a hit".

"Our culture isn't perfect," he said.

"We're going to work as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been."

Live Moment Catch up up the key moments from Dean Cox and Callum Mills's press conference from Swans HQ. The press conference is over Dean Cox and Callum Mills have finished answering questions at Swans HQ. Cox's message to Sydney's fans ahead of the weekend Cox is asked what his message is to the club's fans considering coming to this weekend's games. "I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs. "We want to show that on Sunday." Is there concern for the mental health of the players? Mills is asked whether he is concerned for the mental health of the players suspended by the club. "There's concern in every part. That's the women in the community, our players involved, the women involved. "The wellbeing of everyone involved is [of] the utmost importance." Show more
